pages.description: H.R.1834 would have extended for three years the enhanced health insurance subsidies that help people buy private coverage through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. The extension would have kept these subsidies available to households earning more than four times the federal poverty level, who would otherwise have lost them.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Restore the larger Affordable Care Act (ACA) insurance tax credits for 2026–2028, lowering eligible people's insurance bills and helping them keep coverage. The enhancements “expired on December 31, 2025” [1]. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) says H.R.1834 “would authorize an extension through 2028 of the premium tax credit structure” [2]. The bill applies “to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [3] The credit “reduces out−of-pocket costs for the premiums” [2], and CBO expects the bill to “increase the number of people with health insurance” [2].

points.title: It helps farms that protect soil, water, and wildlife keep going.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps farms that protect soil, water, and wildlife keep going.

  • Because Farmer Liz Krug links the enhanced credits to staying on her farm and caring for its land: “make sure that we’re stewarding this land, and really one of the only options to do that is through the ACA tax credits.” [4]
  • Because The cost relief reaches organic growers. The Kimballs run “a USDA-certified organic fruit, vegetable, and flower farm” [5]. Without an extension, “They’re bracing for an increase in their monthly expenses next year if the premium tax credits end.” [5]
  • Because USDA requires organic farm plans to address “maintaining or improving all natural resources, including soil, water, wetlands, woodlands, and wildlife” [6].
  • Because A 42-year Swiss field study compared organic and conventional plots growing the same sequence of crops. It found: “Organic systems used 92% less pesticides and 76% less mineral nitrogen than conventional systems.” [7] The organic systems also showed “enhanced soil health, richness of micro- and macrofauna and weed species” [7]—healthier soil and more kinds of plants and animals.
  • Because Affordable coverage also helps organic farms keep workers. Harvest Tide Organics' owner explained: “Allen says many of her employees and other farmers rely on individual market coverage for healthcare.” [8] “If the credits do expire and costs skyrocket, Allen says she may lose employees.” [8]
  • So Lower insurance bills help these farms keep owners and workers on the land. Supporting their care for soil, water, and wildlife serves [NAME]'s concern for nature.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Reported farm-level figures vary. The Kimballs' premium was estimated to rise from $450 to $500 a month. Krug reported health costs of about 8% of income, possibly reaching 50% without subsidies, and listed an off-farm job among her options. Harvest Tide's owner reported about a $6,000 yearly increase. None of the accounts names a specific conservation practice that would stop. USDA organic-plan rules apply with or without the bill. Sources: [5], [4], [8], [6].

points.title: It lowers a barrier to running businesses that offer less polluting energy.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It lowers a barrier to running businesses that offer less polluting energy.

  • Because Enhanced credits lower costs for eligible business owners. An analysis of their effects found that “the enhanced premium tax credits would decrease health insurance premiums” [9].
  • Because Insurance costs have threatened this work before. In 2017, owners of a business offering solar power options wrote: “Insurance costs were definitely the deciding factor in whether we would be able to continue our mission” [10]. They explained: “The Affordable Care Act came to our rescue in 2014. We’re still able to offer clean living options and solar opportunities to our neighbors, local businesses and even our town” [10]. That account concerns the original ACA, not the later enhancement; it shows how insurance costs can weigh on such a business, not what the enhancement itself did.
  • Because Solar panels offer electricity with less climate pollution than coal over their whole life. A national laboratory's review found: “Total life cycle GHG emissions from solar PV systems are similar to other renewables and nuclear energy, and much lower than coal.” [11]
  • So Lower premiums ease this kind of insurance-cost barrier for eligible owners doing this work. Helping them keep offering less polluting energy options serves [NAME]'s wish to protect the environment from pollution.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The solar owners' letter is dated March 2017 and concerns ACA coverage from 2014. The enhanced credits were first enacted in 2021. Without the bill, smaller credits and the earlier income cap remain. Sources: [10], [5], [12].

points.title: It makes paid wildlife habitat work easier to take on.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It makes paid wildlife habitat work easier to take on.

  • Because A seasonal job at the National Elk Refuge leaves workers to arrange coverage: “Health insurance, relocation and other benefits are NOT provided.” [13]
  • Because The job maintains a system that “irrigates 4,000 acres of grasslands crucial to winter range habitat on the National Elk Refuge.” [13]
  • So For an eligible worker buying ACA coverage, larger credits lower a personal cost of taking this job. Making habitat care easier to take on serves [NAME]'s concern for wildlife.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The refuge listing pays $16 to $18 an hour at a 40-hour weekly minimum for a season starting between mid-April and late May and ending between mid-August and mid-October, or about $7,000 to $19,000 at minimum hours. The credit requires annual household income of at least 100% of poverty, about $15,650 for one person. The listing does not report workers' other income, household income or coverage. Sources: [13], [14], [15].

points.title: It lowers the cost of protecting oneself against medical bills while volunteering to defend nature.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It lowers the cost of protecting oneself against medical bills while volunteering to defend nature.

  • Because Conservation volunteers face injury risks and personal medical costs. The Nature Conservancy's agreement states: “My activities as a volunteer may involve sustained strenuous physical activity and entail a risk of injury or death.” [16] Volunteers accept that “I am solely responsible for any costs incurred for any medical care received by me” [16].
  • Because Volunteers are encouraged to insure against those medical costs. The agreement says: “TNC expects and encourages me to obtain my own health insurance coverage to the extent I deem appropriate” [16].
  • Because Conservation volunteering directly protects nature. The National Park Service credits volunteer restoration events with “immense benefit to stream health and habitat quality” [17].
  • So Larger credits make personal coverage less costly for eligible volunteers who buy it through the ACA. That eases a personal risk of taking part in activities to defend nature, which [NAME] values.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Nature Conservancy's agreement encourages insurance 'to the extent I deem appropriate' and does not make it a condition of volunteering. The agreement and the restoration report do not say whether volunteers use Marketplace coverage or how coverage bears on volunteering. Sources: [16], [17].

points.title: It helps protect access to a treatment that can avoid pollution from diabetes complications.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It helps protect access to a treatment that can avoid pollution from diabetes complications.

  • Because SGLT2 inhibitors are medicines that help protect kidneys and prevent hospital stays: “SGLT2 inhibitors are now widely used to reduce the risk of hospital admission and kidney failure in people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease.” [18]
  • Because Insurance helps pay for these medicines. A U.S. prescription-cost study found that “insurance coverage for therapy was generally substantial” [19], while “out-of-pocket costs for uninsured individuals was high with an estimated average cost of $138 per month” [19].
  • Because A study used a medical trial to estimate the combined climate pollution from making the medicine, hospital stays, and dialysis, a treatment for failed kidneys. It found: “Despite the greenhouse gas emissions associated with SGLT2 inhibitor production, the total emissions contribution was 20% lower in the treatment group” [18].
  • So Helping people keep insurance protects access to these medicines and the route they offer to less pollution from hospital stays and kidney failure. Preventing that pollution serves [NAME]'s wish to protect the environment.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The SGLT2 cost study covers only people who received therapy and could not account for premiums, deductibles or rebates. The emissions estimate compares canagliflozin with placebo in a trial of type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease and counts assessable emissions only. Sources: [19], [18].

points.title: It reduces the risk of extra driving pollution when local health services close.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It reduces the risk of extra driving pollution when local health services close.

  • Because Credit expiration threatens hospital income. A Commonwealth Fund analysis explains: “These coverage losses would reduce total spending on hospital services” [15].
  • Because Lost income and unpaid bills threaten local services: “further reductions in revenue and increases in uncompensated care could force hospitals to reduce costs by eliminating services” [15].
  • So Restoring the credits eases a source of financial pressure to cut local care.
  • Because Lost nearby care adds driving pollution. A Maine study estimated travel emissions after three maternity units closed in 2023: “the combined additional mileage would have generated about 60.07 metric tons of climate-warming CO2e emissions” [20] in the following year. CO2e puts different warming gases on the same scale.
  • So Reducing the risk of service cuts helps guard against longer journeys and their climate pollution. Avoiding that pollution serves [NAME]'s concern for nature.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The hospital forecast assumes expiration leading to 4.8 million more uninsured people in 2026. CBO, assuming January 2026 enactment, projects 0.1 million more insured in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028 and 1.1 million in 2029. The Maine estimate concerns three maternity closures in 2023 and totals about 60 metric tons of CO2e. Sources: [15], [2], [20].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect The bill restores extra help paying health insurance premiums for 2026–2028. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) describes an “extension through 2028” [2]. The bill applies to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [3].

  • Because Assuming enactment in January 2026, CBO projects more people with insurance than under existing law: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.” [2]
  • Because Insurance increases use of care. Oregon's insurance lottery study found “substantively and statistically significantly higher health care utilization (including primary and preventive care as well as hospitalizations)” [21].
  • Because An analysis comparing extended credits with expiration projects less care without them: “lower revenue for health care providers and fewer services rendered” [22]. Restoring the credits supports the care those losses would otherwise reduce.
  • Because Providing care requires energy and manufactured supplies. U.S. research identifies “indirect emissions that occur as a consequence of producing the electricity and materials that those facilities use” [23].
  • So The bill supports more treatment and prescriptions, adding demand for the energy, supplies and waste disposal traced below.
  • Because For someone committed to protecting nature, a policy's added pollution and habitat damage count as reasons to oppose it.

points.title: Extra care adds climate pollution that threatens habitats and species.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Extra care adds climate pollution that threatens habitats and species.

  • Because Medical facilities and their suppliers release gases that heat the planet: “These emissions arise directly from health care facilities, as well as indirectly from the supply chain of health care goods and services.” [24]
  • Because More of these gases means more warming. Health-care research describes “Changing climate due to an increase in greenhouse gas emissions” [25].
  • Because The UN climate science panel finds that biodiversity loss and damage to ecosystems “will continue to escalate with every increment of global warming (very high confidence)” [26].
  • So The added care brings emissions that increase threats to the natural world [NAME] wants to protect.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: The footprint sources assign emissions by average per-dollar intensity for a past period; one method paper says this approach does not reflect marginal effects. The Oregon study concerns Medicaid coverage for low-income adults. EPA notes that soil buffering can neutralize acid inputs and that mild or moderate coastal nitrogen enrichment can be neutral or positive. Hospitals operate continuously, and some of their footprint is fixed. Sources: [27], [23], [21], [28].

points.title: Extra care adds acid-forming pollution that harms water life and vegetation.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Extra care adds acid-forming pollution that harms water life and vegetation.

  • Because The U.S. health-care footprint includes “acidification (from formation and deposition of acid rain)” [23]. The study traces this burden partly to “electricity use in health care facilities and their supply chains” [23].
  • Because The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports: “Acidification of aquatic ecosystems has been shown to cause direct toxic effects on sensitive aquatic organisms.” [28]
  • Because Acid buildup can leave plants without the nutrients they need by “causing nutrient deficiencies in soils” [28].
  • So Meeting the bill's added demand for care adds pressure on waters, wildlife and vegetation [NAME] wants to defend.

points.title: Extra care adds pollution that forms smog and damages forests.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Extra care adds pollution that forms smog and damages forests.

  • Because The U.S. footprint includes “ground-level ozone (smog) stemming from emissions of criteria air pollutants” [23].
  • Because EPA finds that ozone damages plants and slows their growth: “These injuries can cause stand-level forest decline in sensitive ecosystems.” [28]
  • So The bill's added medical activity contributes to smog that threatens trees and forests [NAME] values.

points.title: Extra care adds nutrient pollution that damages aquatic habitats and changes plant communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Extra care adds nutrient pollution that damages aquatic habitats and changes plant communities.

  • Because The U.S. footprint includes “eutrophication (algae blooms from excess nutrients) in soils and surface waters” [23].
  • Because EPA finds that “too much nitrogen leads to excess production of algae, decreasing water clarity and reducing concentrations of dissolved oxygen” [28].
  • Because The damage includes “habitat loss for fish and shellfish, alteration of food webs, degradation and loss of seagrass beds” [28].
  • Because Added nitrogen also changes which plants thrive on land: “Biological community composition can also change under increased nitrogen loads, as species more tolerant of high-nitrogen conditions out-compete those less tolerant.” [28]
  • So Added nutrient pollution threatens both aquatic habitats and the variety of plants [NAME] wants to protect.

points.title: Extra prescriptions add drug pollution that harms wildlife.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Extra prescriptions add drug pollution that harms wildlife.

  • Because The Oregon insurance study found “substantial and (mostly) statistically significant increases in prescription drugs and outpatient use.” [21]
  • Because Drug use and disposal release residues into nature. A review identifies “rising local pollution levels emanating from patient excreta and inappropriate disposal” [29].
  • Because Making medicines adds another source of pollution. The review describes “the considerable manufacturing pollution externalities created through globalising their supply chains” [29].
  • Because These chemicals damage nature: “their contamination of global waterways is threatening environmental and human health, contributing to biodiversity loss” [29].
  • So The bill supports more drug use and production, adding water pollution that threatens wild species.

points.title: Extra care adds toxic chemical pollution and hazardous waste.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Extra care adds toxic chemical pollution and hazardous waste.

  • Because A U.S. study of 2013 health care traces chemical harm to water life mainly to waste handling: “the most important EIOLCA sector ‘Waste management and remediation’, which contributed more than 85% of the total to ecotoxicity” [23].
  • Because Medical waste includes “solvents and reagents used for laboratory preparations, disinfectants, sterilants and heavy metals contained in medical devices” [30].
  • Because Waste treatment can spread poisons. A World Health Organization global fact sheet warns: “Incineration of heavy metals or materials with high metal content (in particular lead, mercury and cadmium) can lead to the spread of toxic metals in the environment.” [30]
  • So More care adds chemical pollution and hazardous material to handle, increasing threats to the waters and wildlife [NAME] wants to protect.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s incineration and hazardous-handling steps do not establish that added U.S. medical waste follows those harmful routes.

  • Because The World Health Organization (WHO) ties its warning about disinfectants to poor handling: “if those substances are not handled, stored and disposed in an environmentally sound manner” [30].
  • Because U.S. waste treatment does not follow a single route. EPA reports that tighter incinerator standards led to “an increase in the use of alternative technologies for treating medical waste” [31], including “Steam sterilization, such as autoclaving” [31]. Treated waste can then go to “solid waste in landfills or incinerators” [31].
  • Because WHO states: “Measures to ensure the safe and environmentally sound management of health care wastes can prevent adverse health and environmental impacts from such waste including the unintended release of chemical or biological hazards.” [30]
  • So A global list of hazardous materials and possible releases does not show that the bill’s added waste follows those routes in the United States. This response does not answer the PRO’s separate U.S. footprint estimate, which attributes most ecotoxicity to waste management.

points.title: Extra care adds lasting plastic waste that threatens habitats.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Extra care adds lasting plastic waste that threatens habitats.

  • Because Care uses plastic “syringes, intravenous bags, catheters, test kits, and gloves” [32].
  • Because Much U.S. protective gear is thrown away after use and breaks down slowly: it is “designed for single use and is made from polypropylene nonwoven fabrics that have poor biodegradability” [32].
  • Because Health-care waste already reaches land and oceans. The same article describes “dumping domestic and international health care waste into the earth’s terra firma and oceans” [32].
  • Because The U.S. ocean agency explains a physical danger from this waste: “Plastic marine debris can smother wildlife, restricting the flow of oxygen” [33].
  • So Added disposable supplies create more lasting waste and more risk to the natural habitats [NAME] wants to keep free of pollution.
points.con_html:
Response Plastic persistence does not establish an added flow of U.S. medical plastic into habitats under this bill.

  • Because The article’s disposal figure pools all plastics and two destinations: “91% of plastics, including those used in health care, are not recycled and either reside in landfills or have infiltrated natural environments.” [32]
  • Because The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) describes treated medical waste going to “solid waste in landfills or incinerators” [31]. Neither is open habitat.
  • Because The U.S. ocean agency’s cited harm concerns plastic already in the ocean: “Plastic marine debris can smother wildlife, restricting the flow of oxygen” [33].
  • So The article’s broad dumping claim and pooled disposal figure do not establish how added U.S. medical supplies reach habitats. The ocean agency explains what escaped debris can do; it does not establish that the credits increase that escape or its risk.

points.title: Extra care adds demand for water needed by natural habitats.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Extra care adds demand for water needed by natural habitats.

  • Because Treatment uses water, including to clean medical equipment. EPA explains that “Steam sterilizers can use water in three ways” [34].
  • Because Producing supplies also uses scarce water. Global health-care research counts “scarce water use” [25] and finds that water-use impacts “enter health-care operations mainly through supply chains” [25].
  • Because Taking water can worsen existing shortages: “Abstraction of water can magnify the impacts of water stress.” [35]
  • Because Those shortages harm nature: “Water stress also impacts aquatic and water-dependent ecosystems and the ecosystem services they deliver.” [35]
  • So The bill's added care increases water demand in facilities and their supply chains, adding pressure on freshwater habitats where water is scarce.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s facility water step does not establish added loss of water to stressed freshwater habitats.

  • Because Some equipment uses water regardless of patient volume: “some older models have tempering water that flows constantly, even if the unit is turned off or in idle mode” [34].
  • Because Water use is not the same as water lost to the local river system. Water-scarcity guidance explains that “water withdrawn from the environment and released in the same watershed (for cooling purposes for example) does not generally contribute to local water scarcity” [36].
  • So Water flowing through hospital equipment does not establish added water loss where it deprives ecosystems. This response does not answer the PRO’s separate step about “scarce water use” [25] in supply chains.

points.title: Extra care adds demand for mining that damages habitats.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 Extra care adds demand for mining that damages habitats.

  • Because Medical supplies and energy depend on “extraction of raw ores, coal, oil, and gas” [25].
  • Because Demand drives extraction: “Mining is rapidly expanding globally to meet growing demand for metal minerals and construction materials.” [37]
  • Because This damages nature: “Mining is a key driver of land-use change and environmental degradation globally” [37].
  • So Greater demand for medical goods and energy adds pressure to mine and disturb habitats [NAME] wants to preserve.

points.title: Extra hospital care adds a risk to the ozone layer and aquatic food webs.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 Extra hospital care adds a risk to the ozone layer and aquatic food webs.

  • Because More hospital treatment creates more occasions to use gases that block pain. A review lists nitrous oxide among them: “Inhaled anaesthetics are potent greenhouse gases, including nitrous oxide (N 2 O)” [38].
  • Because Using the gas in treatment releases it, though this is the smaller route: “Although not the primary driver of healthcare-related N 2 O consumption, the direct clinical use of N 2 O does contribute to subsequent GHG emissions” [38].
  • Because This gas also damages the protective ozone layer high in the atmosphere: “Nitrous oxide contributes to the destruction of the ozone layer” [38].
  • Because Ozone loss lets through more harmful ultraviolet sunlight (UVB), which reduces growth of tiny aquatic organisms called phytoplankton: “Scientists have demonstrated a direct reduction in phytoplankton production due to ozone depletion-related increases in UVB.” [39]
  • Because These organisms support other water life: “Phytoplankton form the foundation of aquatic food webs.” [39]
  • So By supporting more hospital care, the bill adds occasions for ozone-damaging emissions that threaten aquatic life [NAME] wants to protect.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The footprint sources assign emissions by average per-dollar intensity for a past period; one method paper says this approach does not reflect marginal effects. The Oregon study concerns Medicaid coverage for low-income adults. EPA notes that soil buffering can neutralize acid inputs and that mild or moderate coastal nitrogen enrichment can be neutral or positive. Hospitals operate continuously, and some of their footprint is fixed. Sources: [27], [23], [21], [28].

Evidence note: Across 47 U.S. hospitals, median clinical use was 6.6% of procured nitrous oxide (range 0.2–52.8%), with the rest lost outside clinical use. The review describes the gas as occasionally used as an adjunct to general anaesthesia or for labour analgesia. Clinical use fell 63.8% across departments moving to portable supply. Oregon's hospital results exclude childbirth, and its most common admissions were for mental disorders, skin infections, diabetes complications and alcohol-related disorders. A study of Medicaid expansions found fewer preventable hospitalizations, while Oregon found more admissions overall. Sources: [38], [21], [40].

pages.description: H.R.1834 would have extended for three years the enhanced health insurance subsidies that help people buy private coverage through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. The extension would have kept these subsidies available to households earning more than four times the federal poverty level, who would otherwise have lost them.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, the bill restores larger Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits for 2026–2028. These help eligible people pay monthly bills for insurance bought through the ACA marketplaces. “Congress allowed the enhancements to expire on January 1.” [1] CBO describes an “extension through 2028 of the premium tax credit structure” [2], applying to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [3]

points.title: It protects people who would otherwise lack insurance from untreated illness and medical bills.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It protects people who would otherwise lack insurance from untreated illness and medical bills.

  • Because Assuming enactment in January 2026, CBO projects that the bill would increase the number insured by “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.” [2]
  • Because Insurance makes needed care more accessible: “people who are uninsured get far less needed care and live sicker, shorter lives.” [4]
  • Because For many women, ACA coverage provides access to “preventive services like mammograms, Pap tests, and prenatal care.” [5]
  • Because A randomized study of IRS letters encouraging insurance enrollment found increased coverage and “reduced mortality among middle-aged adults over the same time period.” [6]
  • Because Coverage also “protects people against the health and financial risks of accidents or unexpected illnesses, and it helps people with chronic health needs afford care.” [1]
  • Because The bill also increases public coverage: CBO projects “0.4 million more people would be enrolled in Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program” [2] combined in 2028.
  • Because A randomized Oregon study found that “Medicaid coverage led to a reduction in financial strain from medical costs, according to a number of self-reported measures.” [7]
  • So Bringing more people into coverage protects those exposed to untreated illness, early death and financial hardship. Protecting vulnerable people gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
  • Because Access to treatment also supports work and study. One interviewed enrollee received mental health treatment that “kept her on track as she juggled multiple jobs in the gig economy and completed classes to become a certified nursing assistant.” [8]
  • So Keeping treatment within reach helps stop illness from blocking work and education, advancing the equal opportunities [NAME] values.
  • Because Replacement coverage matters when people lose jobs. Earlier enhanced credits “enabled many who lost ESI to afford new coverage.” [9] ESI means insurance provided through a job.
  • Because Some families have few public alternatives. For one Texas family buying ACA coverage, “In other states, her kids might qualify for free or low-cost health insurance through Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program, but in Texas, their income is too high.” [8]
  • Because Some veterans also need this alternative: Veterans Affairs “services can be inaccessible for those who do not live near VA facilities.” [10] Urban Institute research found that “the expiration of enhanced PTCs would lead to lower enrollment” [10] in subsidized marketplace coverage among veterans.
  • So Restoring affordable coverage protects people exposed by job loss, narrow public insurance rules or gaps in veterans’ care, reinforcing [NAME]’s reason to favor it.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: CBO assumes January 2026 enactment and projects 0.1 million more insured in 2026, with gross benchmark premiums unchanged in 2026. The IRS-letter mortality study warns its estimate may not reflect coverage effects for the remaining uninsured population. Some enrollees keep access to zero-premium plans without the enhancements. In a California trial, emails raised enrollment in plans covering 94% of costs by 3.1 percentage points. Sources: [2], [6], [11], [12].

points.title: It leaves households more money for food, housing and other basic needs.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It leaves households more money for food, housing and other basic needs.

  • Because The credits replace money households must otherwise spend themselves: “PTCs cover premium amounts that people would otherwise be required to pay out of pocket to keep their coverage.” [1]
  • Because The help reaches people with small budgets: “With the enhanced subsidies, most enrollees at the lowest income level — under 150 percent of poverty — pay little or nothing for their plan.” [4]
  • Because An interviewed enrollee explained that higher insurance bills would require him to “cut costs elsewhere and that's now digging into basic necessities, like, food, car, gas, rent.” [8]
  • So Lower insurance payments leave more of these households’ budgets for basic needs. Protecting financially vulnerable people from those sacrifices gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

points.title: It helps insured people choose plans with lower bills when they need treatment.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It helps insured people choose plans with lower bills when they need treatment.

  • Because Larger credits make such plans easier to buy: “While enhanced PTCs do not directly alter patient cost sharing, they allow people to enroll in or switch to plans that have lower cost-sharing obligations.” [4] These are the charges patients pay when they receive care.
  • Because Treatment costs block needed care. With fewer financial resources, “women are already more likely than men to forego or delay health care due to cost” [13].
  • So Helping people buy plans with lower treatment bills reduces a barrier between having insurance and receiving care. Protecting people with little money and substantial health needs gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

points.title: It reduces coverage barriers tied to discrimination and unequal earnings.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It reduces coverage barriers tied to discrimination and unequal earnings.

  • Because A CBPP analysis identifies an unequal effect of losing the enhanced credits: “Black and Latino people will disproportionately lose coverage, which will increase existing racial disparities in health insurance coverage.” [8]
  • Because Unequal pay makes coverage harder to afford: “women, particularly women of color, and LGBTQ+ people are more likely to have lower incomes due to gender and racial pay discrimination and overrepresentation in low-paid jobs” [13].
  • Because The enhanced credits reach these groups. When introduced in 2021, “over 200,000 LGBTQ+ enrollees were eligible for zero-premium plans.” [13]
  • So Restoring help with insurance costs reduces the effect of unequal earnings on access to care and counters coverage losses that widen racial gaps. More equal access for people facing these disadvantages gives [NAME] a reason grounded in equal opportunity and just treatment.

In a California trial, emails raised enrollment in plans covering 94% of costs by 3.1 percentage points. Sources: [2], [6], [11], [12].

Evidence note: A 2026 restriction removes subsidized Marketplace eligibility for lawfully present immigrants with incomes under 100% of poverty. The bill does not change this. The LGBTQ+ count is from 2021. Sources: [14], [13].

points.title: It replaces an abrupt income cutoff with help tied to income and insurance costs.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It replaces an abrupt income cutoff with help tied to income and insurance costs.

  • Because Without the extension, eligibility ends at 400 percent of the federal poverty level: “the tax credit falls suddenly to zero when income crosses this line.” [15]
  • Because With enhanced credits, help remains limited by income, but “it just phases out gradually rather than dropping off suddenly.” [15]
  • Because The restored credit caps eligible households’ payments for the benchmark plan—the plan used to set the credit—at “8.5% of income” [16]. Credits limit payments for “a specific plan, called a benchmark” [17].
  • Because High prices make the cutoff especially harmful. In Urban’s 2026 example, a 60-year-old in Cheyenne earning $65,000 “would face a premium of $26,180—40 percent of their income.” [18] At 8.5 percent, the annual payment for benchmark coverage would be $5,525.
  • Because The cutoff falls especially heavily on “older people, those in high-premium areas (which are heavily rural areas), and small business owners.” [15]
  • So Restoring income-based help protects people from high bills tied to age or location. A gradual phaseout also treats people with nearly identical incomes more equally, giving [NAME] a reason grounded in fair treatment.
  • Because Credits are paid before final annual income is known: “The credit amounts then need to be reconciled with actual income at year’s end when enrollees file their federal taxes.” [4]
  • Because The cutoff creates the risk that “a small income change triggers a large tax liability.” [15]
  • So Removing that cutoff also protects households from a sudden repayment bill caused by barely crossing the income line.

points.title: It makes public help fairer for people whose work does not provide affordable insurance.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It makes public help fairer for people whose work does not provide affordable insurance.

  • Because Many people must arrange coverage themselves: “people who own small businesses or are self-employed typically purchase insurance on their own.” [19]
  • Because People with insurance from a job get a tax break for it: “the tax exclusion for employer coverage.” [15]
  • Because The marketplace credit fills a different gap: “With or without the enhancements, the PTC is available only to people without other affordable coverage options.” [15] The bill restores the “Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [3].
  • So Restoring help above the cutoff reduces the disadvantage of being left to buy insurance yourself while job-based coverage receives tax help. Fairer access to public support across types of work gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

Evidence note: Self-employed people may be able to deduct health insurance premiums. Urban reports that for those beyond the cliff, the enhanced credit is already smaller on average than the tax benefit from the employer exclusion. Sources: [20], [15].

points.title: It protects access for other insurance buyers by supporting a larger, healthier market.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It protects access for other insurance buyers by supporting a larger, healthier market.

  • Because CBO projects full benchmark prices would be “lower by 5.7 percent, 9.0 percent, and 3.3 percent” [2] in 2027, 2028 and 2029, respectively, compared with current-law projections.
  • Because CBO attributes the decline to a healthier mix of buyers: “the people who enroll in the marketplaces would be healthier than would be the case” [2] without the extension.
  • Because This helps buyers who receive no credit: “Even those not eligible for PTCs see lower premiums with enhanced PTCs because the additional enrollment has improved the nongroup market risk pool.” [21]
  • So Bringing healthier buyers into the same market spreads medical costs and lowers the price others must pay themselves. Reducing their barriers to coverage gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
  • Because CBO also projects “6.2 million more people would be enrolled through the health insurance marketplaces” [2] in 2028.
  • Because A smaller market threatens continued access: “A smaller market would in turn discourage competition, since there would be less incentive for multiple insurers to offer coverage to fewer people, and the marketplaces would be more vulnerable to disruption if an insurer leaves.” [4]
  • So Supporting a larger market also reduces the risk that fewer insurance choices disrupt access to care, reinforcing this protection for people who rely on the market.

points.title: It reduces pressure to cut local health services and the jobs and public services their spending supports.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It reduces pressure to cut local health services and the jobs and public services their spending supports.

  • Because Insurance coverage supports payments for care. Urban’s study of credit expiration explains that “lower spending on health care services means lower revenue for health care providers and fewer services rendered” [22].
  • Because Further financial losses at rural hospitals “could force hospitals to reduce costs by eliminating services that would affect all members of their community.” [23]
  • Because Low-income patients also depend on exposed clinics: “Community health centers serve people regardless of their ability to pay, but as patients lose insurance, these providers will struggle to continue meeting their health needs” [24].
  • So By increasing coverage, the bill reduces pressure from unpaid care and lost revenue. Protecting local services also protects patients outside the marketplaces, giving [NAME] a reason to favor it.
  • Because The same revenue supports workers and suppliers: “Health care providers that lose revenue must reduce how much they can spend on their staff and goods purchased from vendors, including medical supplies, technology, consulting, and capital.” [25]
  • Because “Reductions in labor expenses mean that some jobs are lost and some staff may be paid less.” [25]
  • So Reducing this pressure protects workers’ livelihoods and their households from hardship.
  • Because Lost earnings also affect shared services: “The combined reductions in individual and business incomes inevitably lead to lower state and local tax revenues.” [25]
  • Because Those losses make it harder to “continue paying for crucial services like education.” [26]
  • So Supporting paid care also protects the local income and tax revenue behind public services. This extends the bill’s protection of vulnerable people and opportunities beyond its direct recipients.

Urban's provider study compares extension with expiration holding other policies fixed. Community health centers face other coverage losses from separate policies. Sources: [25], [22], [24].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Restore the larger Affordable Care Act (ACA) health-insurance tax credits for 2026–2028. CBO describes an “extension through 2028 of the premium tax credit structure” [2]; the bill applies to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [3]. The extension adds borrowing: “the House-passed bill would increase the deficit by more than $80 billion” [27]. A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue.

points.title: The bill extends public aid to some high-income households while leaving some of the poorest uninsured people without help.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill extends public aid to some high-income households while leaving some of the poorest uninsured people without help.

  • Because Urban Institute projects that a small group with incomes above ten times the federal poverty line would get credits in 2026: “fewer than 13,000 people nationwide” [18] with incomes “over 10 times the FPL would receive the tax credit.” [18]. Their credit would average “$3,410 per person” [18].
  • Because Some uninsured poor people in states that have not expanded Medicaid, the public health-insurance program, are “ineligible for both Medicaid and ACA marketplace subsidies” [28]. The same source counts “1.4 million uninsured individuals” [28] in this gap. The bill leaves that gap in place; it extends the credits “with no additional reforms or changes to the program.” [29].
  • Because Protecting the weakest and giving people equal opportunities calls for putting basic protection for those without it ahead of extra aid for people far above poverty.
  • So Adding aid for that high-income group while keeping these poorest people excluded enlarges an unfair gap in public help. [NAME] has a reason to oppose that choice.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not show that the credit rules unfairly favor wealth over need.

  • Because Eligibility reflects both income and insurance costs. Urban Institute explains that “eligibility is still capped, since the credit phases out as income increases.” [18]
  • Because Higher-income recipients qualify because they face higher premiums; they are “generally older adults and those in high-premium areas.” [18]
  • Because The credits fill a gap in access to affordable insurance: “With or without the enhancements, the PTC is available only to people without other affordable coverage options.” [15] PTC means premium tax credit, or help paying insurance premiums.
  • Because The poorest group's exclusion comes from existing Medicaid and tax-credit rules. The cited source describes them as “ineligible for both Medicaid and ACA marketplace subsidies” [28]. The extension makes “no additional reforms or changes to the program.” [29] The bill leaves that group's position unchanged.
  • So Different amounts of help do not by themselves show unequal concern when insurance costs and other coverage options differ. The PRO does not explain why this rule unjustly favors wealth. The coverage gap is a real unmet need, but it comes from rules the bill does not change.

points.title: Expanding fully paid insurance premiums exposes vulnerable people to broker abuse that disrupts treatment and creates unexpected debts.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Expanding fully paid insurance premiums exposes vulnerable people to broker abuse that disrupts treatment and creates unexpected debts.

  • Because The enhanced credits increased aid enough to provide “access to plans with no premium contributions for those earning 100 to 150 percent of the federal poverty level.” [30]. Restoring that aid expands the plans people can obtain without a monthly payment.
  • Because Brokers can earn money from enrollments that consumers do not discover: “with no monthly bill, consumers have few ways of knowing they're in a plan.” [31]. The payment incentive lasts while coverage continues: “The most common way agents receive commission is on a per-member, per-month basis.” [32].
  • Because Enrollment or plan changes without consent can hurt consumers. GAO lists “loss of access to medical providers and medications, higher copayments and deductibles, or repayment of APTC if income or other eligibility was misrepresented.” [30]. APTC is the tax credit paid to an insurer in advance.
  • Because Broker abuse can also replace care that homeless people already receive. A 2023 report describes one homeless woman's loss of free treatment after she was induced to enroll using false information: “Signing up for private insurance disqualified her from Ryan White coverage.” [32]. The report records the result: “she went without medication for days” [32].
  • Because These tax debts face fewer limits under the law in force in January 2026. The IRS reports “removing the limitations on repayment of excess advance payments of the premium tax credit for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2025.” [33]. Larger advance credits increase the money at stake when an ineligible enrollment remains uncorrected.
  • Note Verification calls leave a route for abuse. December 2025 reporting explains: “Also, new ACA applicants were exempt from the three-way call rule, which leaves open the possibility of agents saying it’s a new consumer when it isn’t.” [34].
  • Note A planned monthly charge to alert people to automatic enrollment was blocked before the vote: “the court temporarily blocked a requirement that returning Marketplace enrollees who would otherwise be automatically reenrolled into a zero-premium plan pay a new five-dollar monthly premium until they actively reenroll.” [35]. H.R.1834 adds “no additional reforms or changes to the program.” [29].
  • So The bill expands a route to enrollment that victims can miss until treatment stops or a tax bill arrives. Protecting people who depend on steady care and cannot absorb unexpected debts gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added exposure.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's examples do not establish that larger credits add abuse or victim debts under the rules in force on January 8.

  • Because GAO tested failures in enrollment checks, not how abuse changes with credit amounts. It warns: “The results of our covert testing, while illustrative of potential enrollment control weaknesses, cannot be generalized to the overall enrollment population.” [30]
  • Because GAO's late-2024 applications used a specific opening: “We submitted the applications outside of the open enrollment period, using a special enrollment period for low-income applicants.” [30] That opening had closed: “Starting August 25, 2025, a consumer can no longer qualify for an SEP just because they have a low income.” [35] SEP means a chance to enroll outside the yearly sign-up period. The bill changes credit dates, not enrollment periods: “with no additional reforms or changes to the program.” [29]
  • Because The PRO's December report locates unauthorized switching mainly in the federal enrollment system. In state-run marketplaces, “such issues are not common.” [34] States say they “require more types of authentication” [34]. Both systems used the enhanced credits; their different checks matter to the claimed risk.
  • Because The PRO's larger-debt claim depends on an ineligible enrollment remaining uncorrected. CMS has an established process for correcting unauthorized coverage and its tax records: “These actions include retroactively restoring or cancelling coverage and updating tax forms to ensure consumers do not suffer adverse tax implications when unauthorized activity occurs.” [36] A comparison of victim debts must account for those corrections.
  • So Loopholes in verification calls and the blocked five-dollar charge identify failures in safeguards. They do not establish the added harm from changing credit amounts. Nor does a higher possible repayment on an uncorrected, ineligible policy establish a rise in victim debts. This response does not answer the reporting that plans with no monthly bill make an unwanted enrollment harder to notice; it limits how far the PRO's examples and repayment figure can show added harm under the rules in force.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: KFF analysis finds that almost all (98%) adults who qualified for a free silver plan with enhanced credits would still qualify for a free bronze plan without them. CMS estimates that about 200,000 consumers had a desired plan changed without consent in 2025. Sources: [37], [38].

points.title: The shift away from job-based coverage puts patients' access to their doctors and protection from medical bills at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The shift away from job-based coverage puts patients' access to their doctors and protection from medical bills at risk.

  • Because CBO projects this change under the bill in 2028: “2.1 million fewer people would have employment-based coverage.” [2]. Coverage would move toward the ACA Marketplaces: “6.2 million more people would be enrolled through the health insurance marketplaces” [2].
  • Because KFF's 2024 review reports a broader choice of primary care doctors in large employer plans: “One analysis found that primary care networks for large group plans were 25% larger than those found on the Marketplaces.” [39].
  • Because Changing plans can leave a patient's doctor outside every available Marketplace network. KFF's analysis of 2021 networks explains: “This means that people transitioning to a Marketplace plan from another coverage source may not have been able to find any plan that included their doctor.” [39].
  • Because In KFF's 2023 survey, among Marketplace enrollees whose plan excluded a needed doctor or hospital, “34% said they were unable to get needed care” [39].
  • Because Losing coverage for a doctor affects both care and bills: “Enrollees receiving care from out-of-network providers often face coverage denials or substantially higher out-of-pocket expenses.” [39].
  • So Drawing people away from job plans into this market adds a risk of losing covered access to a treating doctor or paying more to keep that doctor. Protecting sick patients' care and finances gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that risk.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A person claiming the credit must lack an affordable offer that provides minimum value. In its 2022 analysis of a permanent extension, CBO said the job-coverage decline is driven primarily by reduced employer offers, and that few employers changed their decision to offer coverage under the temporary 2021–2022 subsidies. H.R.1834's extension runs through 2028. KFF's 25% network comparison concerns large group plans, its 34% figure applies to enrollees who reported a network problem, and it finds 27% of practicing physicians in no Marketplace network in 2021. Sources: [40], [41], [39].

points.title: Added debt puts future emergency aid under pressure.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Added debt puts future emergency aid under pressure.

  • Because Borrowing adds interest costs. CBO explains: “If federal debt held by the public continued to grow, the government would spend more on interest payments” [42].
  • Because Debt can make lawmakers less willing to borrow for emergencies: “The size of the debt might make lawmakers feel constrained from using deficit-financed fiscal policy to respond to unforeseen events, promote economic activity, or further other goals.” [42].
  • Because Emergency spending includes support for people who lose work or cannot afford food. CBO notes that “downturns have historically prompted lawmakers to enact legislation that further reduces revenues and increases federal spending in an effort to increase people’s income” [42].
  • So Adding debt strengthens a barrier to funding help when people become vulnerable. Preserving that protection gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill's added borrowing.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO's debt passages describe the government's total long-term debt path, with deficits averaging 6.3% of GDP from 2025 to 2055. CBO says the effects of policy changes depend on policy specifics, that fiscal-crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt, and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability of a crisis. Unemployment and food benefits also rise automatically, without new legislation, when more people qualify. CBO scores the bill at about $80.6 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035. Sources: [42], [43], [2].

points.title: Added borrowing puts downward pressure on future workers' pay.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Added borrowing puts downward pressure on future workers' pay.

  • Because Federal borrowing competes for money that businesses could invest: “The increased federal borrowing associated with larger amounts of debt reduces the resources available for private investment.” [42].
  • Because Less investment leaves workers with fewer tools and other resources. CBO explains: “Consequently, they would be less productive, their compensation would be lower, and they would therefore be less inclined to work.” [42].
  • So The bill's added borrowing creates pressure on the earnings future workers need to build secure lives. Concern for their opportunities gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that burden.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO's debt passages describe the government's total long-term debt path, with deficits averaging 6.3% of GDP from 2025 to 2055. CBO says the effects of policy changes depend on policy specifics, that fiscal-crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt, and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability of a crisis. Unemployment and food benefits also rise automatically, without new legislation, when more people qualify. CBO scores the bill at about $80.6 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035. Sources: [42], [43], [2].

points.title: Added debt contributes to financial risks that reach people beyond the United States.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Added debt contributes to financial risks that reach people beyond the United States.

  • Because CBO identifies a risk from growing debt: “The likelihood of a fiscal crisis would increase if federal debt continued to grow faster than GDP, because mounting debt could erode investors’ confidence in the U.S. government’s fiscal position.” [42]. GDP measures the size of the economy.
  • Because A loss of confidence can damage banks and people's savings. CBO explains: “The resulting losses incurred by institutions and businesses—including insurance companies, banks, mutual funds, and pension funds—could be large enough to cause some financial institutions to fail.” [42].
  • Because The harm can cross borders: “such a crisis could spread globally as liquidity declined and financial institutions reduced their lending, leading to an economic contraction.” [42]. In plain terms, money and lending would become harder to obtain and economies would shrink.
  • So The bill adds to debt that creates this risk to savings and livelihoods at home and abroad. Concern for people's security, including strangers in other countries, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added risk.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO's debt passages describe the government's total long-term debt path, with deficits averaging 6.3% of GDP from 2025 to 2055. CBO says the effects of policy changes depend on policy specifics, that fiscal-crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt, and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability of a crisis. Unemployment and food benefits also rise automatically, without new legislation, when more people qualify. CBO scores the bill at about $80.6 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035. Sources: [42], [43], [2].

points.title: Making plans with abortion coverage easier to buy raises a protection concern for unborn children.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Making plans with abortion coverage easier to buy raises a protection concern for unborn children.

  • Because The bill's larger credits help people buy Marketplace plans, and “twelve states now have laws that require all fully-insured group plans and individual plans (including Marketplace plans) to include abortion coverage.” [44].
  • Because Coverage removes a financial barrier to obtaining abortions. Guttmacher reports: “Women who are low-income and lack insurance coverage for abortion often struggle to come up with the money to pay for the procedure.” [45]. Its review of Medicaid restrictions finds that some women “are unable to obtain one because of lack of abortion coverage.” [45].
  • Because The procedure at issue deliberately ends an ongoing pregnancy. WHO defines induced abortion as “the deliberate interruption of an ongoing pregnancy by medical or surgical means” [46].
  • Because Whether unborn children count among the vulnerable is a contested moral premise. A developing human life's inability to speak or act for itself makes it especially dependent on others for protection. If [NAME] accepts that premise, this dependence gives a reason to include unborn children among the vulnerable lives to protect.
  • Note Separate payment rules leave abortion coverage in the plans the bill helps people buy. KFF explains that plans can cover abortions beyond the life-endangerment, rape and incest exceptions, but “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” [44]. The bill increases help buying the plan that includes that coverage.
  • So Helping people obtain coverage for procedures that end developing human lives gives [NAME], on that premise, a reason to oppose the bill out of concern for those lives.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: KFF reports that twelve states require abortion coverage in Marketplace plans, 25 bar it, and 13 and DC neither require nor prohibit it. Federal funds cannot pay for most abortions, and plans covering them charge at least $1 a month, kept in a separate account. The financial-barrier finding comes from a review of Medicaid enrollees subject to the Hyde Amendment. Sources: [44], [45].
