to listen to and understand people who are different to them
to accept people even when they disagree with them
pages.description: H.R.1834 would have extended for three years the enhanced health insurance subsidies that help people buy private coverage through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. The extension would have kept these subsidies available to households earning more than four times the federal poverty level, who would otherwise have lost them.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on January 8, 2026, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Restore the larger Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax credits that lower eligible people's monthly costs for insurance bought through ACA marketplaces, for 2026–2028. The larger credits had expired: “These enhanced premium tax credits expired on December 31, 2025.” [1] The bill extends the rules “through 2028” [2] and applies to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [2] “These credits lower monthly premiums upfront and are calculated based on a consumer's household income and the cost of coverage in their local market.” [1] Assuming enactment in January 2026, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects more people insured: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.” [3]

points.title: It makes acceptance of different identities and ways of life practical through a shared insurance system.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It makes acceptance of different identities and ways of life practical through a shared insurance system.

  • Because The larger premium tax credits (PTCs) help people across racial groups using the same rules: “The enhanced PTCs are not targeted by race or ethnicity, but they are more generous at lower incomes and directly assist those without affordable insurance offers from an employer.” [4]
  • Because A study comparing 2025 coverage with and without the larger credits found benefits for Black and Hispanic people: “Black and Hispanic people will see greater reductions in the percent of uninsured people relative to White people because of enhanced PTCs.” [4]
  • Because The credits also reach different genders and sexual orientations: they have “made Marketplace coverage affordable for women and LGBTQ+ people with low and moderate incomes” [5].
  • Because The same insurance system serves different ways of earning a living. A 2025 analysis estimated that “about 5.2 million small-business owners and self-employed Americans are covered through the marketplaces.” [6]
  • Because ACA coverage also includes people with illnesses they already have, through “guaranteed coverage for preexisting conditions.” [7]
  • Because The same system also serves people across political disagreements. A 2025 survey found “about four in ten Marketplace enrollees (39%) are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents” [8]; “Just over four in ten Marketplace enrollees (45%) identify as Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents, while 17% do not identify or lean toward either political party.” [8]
  • So Restoring the larger credits helps eligible people afford this shared coverage across differences in race, sexual orientation, gender identity, health, work, and politics. Accepting all kinds of people gives [NAME] a reason to help them use a shared institution without making similarity to [NAME] a condition of support.
points.con_html:
Response Helping people across different groups afford insurance does not by itself show that the larger payment puts acceptance of their differences into practice.

  • Because The value framework defines tolerance as “Acceptance and understanding of those who are different from oneself” [9]. It separately defines concern as “Commitment to equality, justice, and protection for all people” [9]. Helping people's welfare cannot simply stand in for accepting their differences.
  • Because The coverage study explains the benefits through income and access to workplace insurance: “The enhanced PTCs are not targeted by race or ethnicity, but they are more generous at lower incomes and directly assist those without affordable insurance offers from an employer.” [4]
  • Because The bill extends the larger credits “with no additional reforms or changes to the program.” [1] The PRO identifies no change in whether identity or similarity to [NAME] is a condition of support.
  • So The PRO links the bill to wider access, then treats support for that access as acceptance of recipients' identities. That last step needs its own reason. Listing recipients' races, genders, sexual orientations, illnesses, jobs, or party labels does not supply it. Neither the current credit nor the extension makes agreement with [NAME] a condition.

points.title: It makes room for reproductive choices [NAME] may disagree with.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It makes room for reproductive choices [NAME] may disagree with.

  • Because The extension keeps the existing rules for plans' benefits: it makes “no additional reforms or changes to the program.” [1]
  • Because Abortion coverage varies by state: “States decide whether insurance covers abortion.” [10] Some states require it: “twelve states now have laws that require all fully-insured group plans and individual plans (including Marketplace plans) to include abortion coverage.” [11]
  • Because For abortions beyond the exceptions for rape, incest, or danger to the pregnant person's life, “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” [11] Plans must “segregate these funds from other premium funds.” [11]
  • So Where these plans are available, restoring the credits makes the whole insurance plan more affordable for eligible people while keeping separate payment for those abortions. Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to support their coverage while leaving room for reproductive choices [NAME] may reject.
points.con_html:
Response The abortion-payment rules explain how support can coexist with disagreement, but do not establish a tolerance-based reason to increase the payment.

  • Because The extension makes “no additional reforms or changes to the program.” [1] It leaves the existing rules for abortion coverage in place.
  • Because For abortions beyond the exceptions for rape, incest, or danger to the pregnant person's life, KFF states that “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” [11] Plans must “segregate these funds from other premium funds.” [11]
  • Because Those rules separate paying for other care from paying for these abortions. They do not connect the size of the federal payment to accepting people who make different reproductive choices.
  • So Making the whole plan cheaper explains the financial benefit. Separate payment explains why support need not endorse abortion. The PRO still needs a reason why accepting the person favors this increase in aid; showing that support is consistent with disagreement does not supply one.

points.title: It helps sustain health centers that listen across language and cultural differences.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It helps sustain health centers that listen across language and cultural differences.

  • Because Community health centers (CHCs) serve people insured through the marketplaces: “Health centers are a principal source of primary care and are essential to provider networks offered by Medicaid managed care organizations and marketplace plans.” [12]
  • Because Federal rules require centers to seek payment for insured patients' care: “The health center must make and continue to make every reasonable effort to collect appropriate reimbursement for its costs” [13].
  • Because Losing insured patients threatens their income: “As patients lose insurance, CHCs will face the prospect of having to meet the health needs of millions of people even as revenue falls.” [12]
  • So Restoring premium help supports these patients' coverage and protects a source of income for their health centers.
  • Because Federal standards require language help: “Health center patients with limited English proficiency are provided with interpretation and translation” [13].
  • Because The standards also require support for staff to provide care “in a manner that is culturally appropriate and bridges linguistic and cultural differences.” [13]
  • Because Providing language support takes “financial and staff resources.” [14]
  • Because Standard board rules give patients a voice in the centers' decisions: “These health center patient board members must, as a group, represent the individuals who are served by the health center.” [13]
  • So Protecting insurance income helps sustain services that let patients explain their needs across language and cultural differences and help shape their care. Supporting that work serves [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand people unlike them.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Federal standards require interpretation services and patient board majorities at health centers under either option. The forecast of falling center revenue concerns overall finances and does not report changes in these specific services. Sources: [13], [12].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, the bill restores larger tax credits—help paying for marketplace health insurance—for 2026–2028. CBO describes “an extension through 2028 of the premium tax credit structure” [3]; the bill applies to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [2]. CBO also projects that in 2028 “2.1 million fewer people would have employment-based coverage.” [3]. Larger credits can reduce employers’ offers of insurance. In its analysis of making the same credit expansion permanent, CBO attributes the decline in job coverage mainly to “a reduction in offers of employment-based coverage that would result from the enhanced marketplace subsidies.” [15].

points.title: The bill increases pressure on people who refuse to pay for abortion coverage on religious grounds.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill increases pressure on people who refuse to pay for abortion coverage on religious grounds.

  • Because New Jersey requires abortion coverage in its regulated plans: “require comprehensive abortion coverage as a part of all health benefits plans regulated by the department.” [16]. This includes marketplace plans: “The individual market includes plans offered on the marketplace, through Get Covered New Jersey, the State’s Official Health Insurance Marketplace, and off the marketplace.” [16].
  • Because In plans covering abortions beyond the federal exceptions for rape, incest or life endangerment, insurers must “Collect from each enrollee” [17] a payment for that coverage. Its minimum is $1 a month: “May not estimate such a cost at less than one dollar per enrollee, per month.” [17].
  • Because New Jersey’s religious exception is for employers: “A religious employer may request, and a carrier shall grant, an exclusion for medical and surgical abortion coverage, if coverage conflicts with the religious employer's bona fide religious beliefs and practices.” [18]. That exception does not give individual marketplace buyers a plan without abortion coverage.
  • So Reducing job coverage also puts workers with that religious exemption at risk of needing a marketplace plan that requires the abortion payment.
  • Because These are documented religious objections. The Alliance of Health Care Sharing Ministries says some religious Americans would reject marketplace insurance “because of conscience objections arising from their religious exercise or expression.” [19].
  • So In such markets, the bill increases the help an eligible objector must pass up to avoid the abortion payment. The pressure grows because the subsidy grows; the bill need not create a new charge.
  • Because Accepting people who disagree includes respecting their refusal to take part in a practice that violates their faith.
  • So Increasing the financial cost of that refusal gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The religious-employer step does not show loss of a fully conscience-compatible plan, and a larger forgone benefit does not by itself weigh against accepting the person who refuses it.

  • Because The bill extends premium help: “Extension of Rules To Increase Premium Assistance Amounts” [2]. The abortion-payment rule already set its floor: “May not estimate such a cost at less than one dollar per enrollee, per month.” [17].
  • Because A larger credit makes enrolling more attractive. The PRO treats that stronger incentive as added pressure on those who refuse. But accepting a person’s refusal does not depend on holding down the benefit available for a choice they reject.
  • Because The religious-employer exception is limited. It cannot exclude “care that is necessary to preserve the life or health of the covered person” [18]. The exception alone does not establish that the job plan avoids all abortion coverage the worker rejects.
  • So The forgone credit is larger for an eligible objector. Whether that counts against accepting them is the disputed step, and the exception does not establish the claimed loss of a conscience-compatible job plan.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO's projection of 2.1 million fewer people with job coverage in 2028 is a national total and does not identify religiously exempt plans. Sources: [3].

points.title: The bill expands public financing of insurance plans that religious taxpayers object to supporting.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill expands public financing of insurance plans that religious taxpayers object to supporting.

  • Because Premium credits finance the plans themselves: “The credits are paid directly to health insurers, who in turn lower the monthly amounts they charge.” [20]. The larger credits also apply to eligible buyers of the abortion-covering plans described above.
  • Because Catholic bishops object specifically to taxpayers financing such plans: “It is also unacceptable to compel taxpayers to subsidize plans that cover abortions.” [21].
  • Note Federal credits cannot pay for abortion coverage beyond the federal exceptions: “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” [11]. Keeping the abortion money separate does not answer the bishops’ stated objection to public financing of the whole plan.
  • Because Tolerance gives [NAME] a reason to respect limits people place on their own participation in a disputed practice, even when [NAME] disagrees with their belief.
  • So Expanding the public financing these taxpayers reject gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The bishops’ objection concerns what other people’s publicly supported plans may cover; accepting the objectors does not make their preferred spending rule a test of tolerance.

  • Because Their requested policy reaches beyond their own insurance: “plans offered by health insurance companies on ACA exchanges cannot cover elective abortion.” [21].
  • Because The rules separate what federal help pays for within those plans. The account for other care must be “used exclusively to pay for services other than the services described in paragraph (d)(1) of this section” [17]—abortions outside the federal funding exceptions.
  • Because The PRO objects to public support for the whole plan. Fund separation identifies what the federal money buys; the decisive gap is between accepting religious taxpayers and adopting their limits on other people’s insurance. The stated value calls for accepting people even when [NAME] disagrees with them.
  • So The objection establishes a disagreement about public spending. Increasing the disputed spending does not by itself establish a failure to accept the people who object.

points.title: The bill widens the financial disadvantage of using religious health sharing instead of marketplace insurance.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill widens the financial disadvantage of using religious health sharing instead of marketplace insurance.

  • Because These groups let members share medical costs: “Members pay to join; the organization uses the collected fees to reimburse members for some health care costs.” [22]. Their rules express a religious practice: “the sharing guidelines are deeply shaped by the shared religious beliefs of the members.” [19].
  • Because They cannot receive the bill’s larger credits: “HCSMs aren't eligible for the tax subsidies that reduce premiums for marketplace plans.” [22].
  • So For a member eligible for marketplace credits, the bill increases the subsidy they forgo when they use religious sharing in place of insurance. It makes that way of practicing their faith less attractive financially.
  • Because Accepting different religious groups includes making room for how they practice their faith. Giving people a larger financial reason to replace that practice puts pressure on that acceptance.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose the larger financial preference against relying on these groups for medical costs.
points.con_html:
Response Different support for marketplace insurance and voluntary religious sharing does not establish less acceptance of a religious community.

  • Because The credit pays for “health insurance obtained through the marketplaces established by the Affordable Care Act.” [3].
  • Because The ministries’ own alliance distinguishes their arrangement from insurance: “There are no contractually required payments by the HCSM.” [19]. A health care sharing ministry helps members share bills voluntarily.
  • Because The distinction concerns the arrangement being funded. Enlarging help to buy insurance does not make its rules a condition of belonging to a religious community. The PRO needs a further premise connecting a stronger incentive to buy this different product with less acceptance of the people who keep sharing bills.
  • So The wider financial gap does not itself establish less acceptance of religious sharing. Respect for its members does not depend on keeping marketplace insurance less affordable.

points.title: The loss of job coverage puts insurance for care required by some Jewish teachings at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The loss of job coverage puts insurance for care required by some Jewish teachings at risk.

  • Because Some job plans cover abortion broadly. KFF’s 2023 survey of firms with at least 200 workers found that “32% cover abortion in most or all circumstances” [23]. Private employers that pay medical bills themselves can escape state insurance restrictions: “This law generally exempts self-funded plans offered by private employers from state insurance regulations.” [23].
  • Because Marketplace rules can exclude abortions needed to protect health. Kansas bars exchange plans from covering abortions it calls elective: “No health insurance exchange established within this state or any health insurance exchange administered by the federal government or its agencies within this state shall offer health insurance contracts, plans, or policies that provide coverage for elective abortions” [24]. Its definition reaches health-protecting abortions that do not prevent death: “"Elective" means an abortion for any reason other than to prevent the death of the mother” [24].
  • Because The Rabbinical Assembly teaches that some abortions are religiously required to protect health: “late-term abortions are allowed and sometimes required, particularly when complications can develop that endanger a woman’s life or health, which includes her physical and mental health and her ability to bear future children.” [25].
  • So Reducing job coverage exposes workers whose employers pay for those abortion benefits directly to replacement marketplace coverage that excludes care their faith requires. This puts insurance that lets them follow their faith at risk.
  • Because Respecting a different faith includes respecting its members’ ability to follow its teachings when they need care.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose putting that coverage at risk.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect the projected drop in job coverage to a greater risk of losing abortion benefits required by the cited Jewish teaching.

  • Because CBO’s 2028 forecast—“2.1 million fewer people would have employment-based coverage.” [3]—counts people in job plans, without identifying the abortion benefits in the coverage that would end.
  • Because KFF’s benefit survey concerns employers “with 200 or more employees” [23]. Its finding that “32% cover abortion in most or all circumstances” [23] describes those firms’ largest plans, not the plans employers would stop offering under this bill.
  • Because The incentives to keep coverage differ by employer size. KFF explains: “Large employers are potentially subject to financial penalty under the ACA if they do not offer health insurance coverage meeting certain requirements to their full-time employees.” [26]. The PRO gives no basis for treating its large-firm benefit survey as a sample of the coverage employers would stop offering.
  • So A benefit survey of large employers and a national enrollment forecast do not establish a shift out of the plans providing the broader abortion benefits. The missing link is evidence of increased risk to that protection, not a count of affected Jewish workers.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: In KFF's 2023 survey of large firms' largest plans, 32% cover abortion in most or all circumstances and 40% of respondents did not know whether their plan covers it. Sources: [23].

points.title: The loss of job coverage puts transgender workers’ transition care at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 The loss of job coverage puts transgender workers’ transition care at risk.

  • Because Job plans can cover care used in a gender transition. KFF reports: “Coverage of gender affirming care services in employer plans is fairly common.” [27].
  • Because Replacement marketplace coverage can exclude it: “In states where coverage for gender-affirming care is not required, some plans may exclude this coverage altogether.” [28]. Under the 2026 rules, even state-required coverage falls outside the federal subsidy: “premium tax credits (PTCs) cannot be used to cover the cost of that care” [29].
  • So The bill’s reduction in job coverage creates a risk that workers whose plans cover transition care will need replacement plans that exclude it. Larger premium credits do not require those plans to cover the missing care.
  • Because Accepting transgender people includes making room for them to live according to their gender identity. Losing coverage for care that supports that identity works against that acceptance.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose this risk to transgender workers’ care.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that the bill makes workers with transition-care coverage more likely to lose that benefit.

  • Because Its employer evidence concerns “large employers (200 or more workers)” [27]. KFF also reports that the largest firms “were significantly more likely to report covering hormone therapy in their largest plan” [27].
  • Because The incentives to keep coverage differ by employer size. KFF explains: “Large employers are potentially subject to financial penalty under the ACA if they do not offer health insurance coverage meeting certain requirements to their full-time employees.” [26] The evidence on who covers this care therefore does not show that those plans are among the ones dropped.
  • So The PRO shows that benefits can differ, but does not connect the bill’s reduction in job coverage to the plans that cover transition care.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: KFF's 'fairly common' rests on 24% of large employers reporting coverage of gender-affirming hormone therapy, with 45% not knowing and 31% not offering it. A CMS provision effective for 2026 bars these procedures as essential health benefits under either option. States can still require Marketplace plans to cover this care, and plans can choose to cover it. Sources: [27], [30], [29].

pages.description: H.R.1834 would have extended for three years the enhanced health insurance subsidies that help people buy private coverage through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. The extension would have kept these subsidies available to households earning more than four times the federal poverty level, who would otherwise have lost them.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, H.R.1834 restores larger Affordable Care Act marketplace tax credits for 2026–2028. These help pay monthly health insurance bills. The enhancements had expired: “Yet Congress allowed the enhancements to expire on January 1.” [1] The bill extends them “through 2028” [2] and applies to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [2] The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) explains that the credit “reduces out−of-pocket costs for the premiums” [3].

points.title: It expands access to care that prevents illness, treats it, and saves lives.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It expands access to care that prevents illness, treats it, and saves lives.

  • Because For enactment in January 2026, CBO projects more insured people than under current law: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.” [3]
  • Because A study compared previously uninsured adults eligible for marketplace help with adults who had steady coverage through work. It found “decreased barriers to medical care” [4].
  • Because Primary care and preventive visits “help prevent and manage costly chronic diseases.” [5]
  • Because A lottery study of Medicaid, public insurance for people with low incomes, found that gaining coverage helped “raise rates of diabetes detection and management” [6].
  • Because Coverage also “protects people against the health and financial risks of accidents or unexpected illnesses” [1].
  • Because The Medicaid lottery found a mental health benefit: “Medicaid coverage led to a substantial reduction in the risk of a positive screening result for depression.” [6]
  • Because A randomized outreach study increased marketplace and Medicaid enrollment. Over two years, “this additional coverage reduced mortality among middle-aged adults over the same time period.” [7]
  • So For an average American who needs Marketplace coverage, now or after a change in work or family circumstances, restoring affordable coverage strengthens access to prevention, medicines, and treatment for ordinary illness and injury risks. That serves [NAME]’s aim to protect physical and mental health and avoid danger to life.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The marketplace study targeted the longer-term uninsured. Oregon participants had been uninsured for six months and received Medicaid with no patient cost-sharing and low premiums. The mortality analysis covered adults aged 45–64 and excluded people with full prior-year coverage. Sources: [4], [6], [7].

Evidence note: These personal benefits are conditional on Marketplace coverage. Census reports employment-based insurance covered 53.8 percent of the population for some or all of 2024. Credit eligibility excludes an affordable employer plan meeting minimum value and eligibility for the listed public programs; H.R.1834 does not change those conditions. The PROs state the buyer condition, and the job-loss and community-service routes have different reach. These facts inform applicability and strength; they do not contradict a benefit within the stated condition. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It helps people who keep insurance afford plans with lower bills when they need care.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps people who keep insurance afford plans with lower bills when they need care.

  • Because Larger premium credits make plans with lower bills for care easier to buy: “they allow people to enroll in or switch to plans that have lower cost-sharing obligations.” [10] These are the amounts patients pay when they get care.
  • Because A national 2024 survey found that many adults whose insurance left care hard to afford skipped needed care: “Nearly three of five (57%) underinsured adults said they avoided getting needed health care because of its cost” [11].
  • Because The same survey reports that “two of five (41%) working-age adults who reported a cost-related delay in their care said a health problem had worsened because of it.” [11]
  • So For an average American buying Marketplace coverage, making a plan with lower treatment bills easier to buy reduces the risk of going without needed care and letting a health problem worsen.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Among underinsured adults in the 2024 survey, 66% had job coverage. The bankruptcy study estimates the combined effect of premium credits and cost-sharing subsidies under the earlier ACA. The follow-up debt study states that observational data cannot prove causality or its direction. Sources: [11], [12], [13].

Evidence note: These personal benefits are conditional on Marketplace coverage. Census reports employment-based insurance covered 53.8 percent of the population for some or all of 2024. Credit eligibility excludes an affordable employer plan meeting minimum value and eligibility for the listed public programs; H.R.1834 does not change those conditions. The PROs state the buyer condition, and the job-loss and community-service routes have different reach. These facts inform applicability and strength; they do not contradict a benefit within the stated condition. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It protects money for food, heat, and housing that support health and personal safety.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects money for food, heat, and housing that support health and personal safety.

  • Because The restored credits pay part of an insurance bill that households would otherwise have to pay themselves: “PTCs cover premium amounts that people would otherwise be required to pay out of pocket to keep their coverage.” [1] PTCs are premium tax credits.
  • Because Subsidized coverage also protects household finances. A study using tax and credit records found that earlier ACA help with premiums and treatment bills “reduced consumer bankruptcies” [12].
  • Because Medical bills crowd out basic needs. In the national 2024 survey, households with medical debt reported that they “were forced to cut back on basic necessities like food, heat, or rent” [11].
  • Because Food and housing insecurity threaten health. A national follow-up study describes these conditions as “associated with adverse health outcomes” [13].
  • So Lower monthly premiums and protection from large medical bills leave more resources for essentials. For an average American buying Marketplace coverage, protecting food and a safe home gives a health and safety reason to favor the bill.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Among underinsured adults in the 2024 survey, 66% had job coverage. The bankruptcy study estimates the combined effect of premium credits and cost-sharing subsidies under the earlier ACA. The follow-up debt study states that observational data cannot prove causality or its direction. Sources: [11], [12], [13].

Evidence note: These personal benefits are conditional on Marketplace coverage. Census reports employment-based insurance covered 53.8 percent of the population for some or all of 2024. Credit eligibility excludes an affordable employer plan meeting minimum value and eligibility for the listed public programs; H.R.1834 does not change those conditions. The PROs state the buyer condition, and the job-loss and community-service routes have different reach. These facts inform applicability and strength; they do not contradict a benefit within the stated condition. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: Lower premiums may protect mental health by easing financial distress.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Lower premiums may protect mental health by easing financial distress.

  • Because The bill restores the extra help introduced in 2021. CBO identifies the extended credits as those provided in the “American Rescue Plan Act of 2021” [3].
  • Because A national panel study compared changes in insurance costs and distress before and after those enhancements, using people insured through work as its comparison group. Its published abstract reports that lower premiums “corresponded with a notable reduction in moderate-to-severe psychological distress.” [14]
  • So For an average American buying Marketplace coverage, restoring that premium relief may protect against harmful distress, including while already insured. That gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The cited abstract does not show that the premium rules renewed by H.R.1834 caused the reported reduction in distress.

  • Because The study compares insurance groups “before and after the ARPA's implementation” [14]. Its abstract reports a change after that law, without reporting a result that separates its premium rules from other changes affecting the groups differently.
  • Because ARPA also “temporarily expanded CSR silver 94 eligibility for the last 6 months of 2021 to all households receiving unemployment insurance regardless of income” [15]. These plans sharply lower bills for treatment, adding another change for affected marketplace households.
  • Because H.R.1834 renews premium rules, including the “Extension of Rules To Increase Premium Assistance Amounts” [2]. It does not renew that temporary expansion of help with treatment bills.
  • So The cited record does not separate the mental-health effect of the renewed premium rules from the effects of the broader 2021 package.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: These personal benefits are conditional on Marketplace coverage. Census reports employment-based insurance covered 53.8 percent of the population for some or all of 2024. Credit eligibility excludes an affordable employer plan meeting minimum value and eligibility for the listed public programs; H.R.1834 does not change those conditions. The PROs state the buyer condition, and the job-loss and community-service routes have different reach. These facts inform applicability and strength; they do not contradict a benefit within the stated condition. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It strengthens the insurance backstop when jobs or incomes change.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It strengthens the insurance backstop when jobs or incomes change.

  • Because Losing work often means losing health insurance: “Job losses often mean losing employer-sponsored insurance, affecting millions of individuals.” [16]
  • Because Larger marketplace subsidies helped replace coverage from work, called ESI: they “enabled many who lost ESI to afford new coverage.” [16]
  • Because The bill also extends help above four times the poverty line through its “Extension of Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line.” [2]
  • Because Without that rule, “the tax credit falls suddenly to zero when income crosses this line.” [17] For credits paid in advance, that cutoff creates a risk that “a small income change triggers a large tax liability.” [17]
  • So A stronger fallback after job loss and removal of this income cutoff reduce threats to affordable coverage and continuing treatment. That protects [NAME]’s health through ordinary changes in work and income.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: KFF's 2021 data show that on average 27% of practicing physicians who submitted Medicare claims were in no Marketplace plan network offered to enrollees that year, so replacement coverage may not include an existing doctor. Sources: [18].

Evidence note: Research using 2014–2019 data found that the risk of losing insurance remained virtually unchanged with the ACA, with a 20% two-year chance of losing coverage for people in Medicaid or private exchanges and 8.5% for those with employer coverage. It studies the earlier ACA, not the enhanced credits. Sources: [19].

points.title: It lowers full insurance prices, helping people who receive no tax credit.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It lowers full insurance prices, helping people who receive no tax credit.

  • Because CBO expects healthier enrollment than without the extension: “on average, the people who enroll in the marketplaces would be healthier” [3].
  • Because CBO therefore projects lower prices before tax credits for benchmark plans, meaning “the mid-level Marketplace plan used to determine how much help people get with premiums” [20]. For 2027, 2028, and 2029, respectively, “they would be lower by 5.7 percent, 9.0 percent, and 3.3 percent” [3].
  • So For an average American buying Marketplace coverage without a tax credit, lower full prices make coverage easier to buy and keep. That protects access to needed care and the health it supports.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: These personal benefits are conditional on Marketplace coverage. Census reports employment-based insurance covered 53.8 percent of the population for some or all of 2024. Credit eligibility excludes an affordable employer plan meeting minimum value and eligibility for the listed public programs; H.R.1834 does not change those conditions. The PROs state the buyer condition, and the job-loss and community-service routes have different reach. These facts inform applicability and strength; they do not contradict a benefit within the stated condition. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It supports a more dependable choice of health plans.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It supports a more dependable choice of health plans.

  • Because CBO projects that, with the bill, “more people would be enrolled through the health insurance marketplaces” [3].
  • Because A larger customer base gives insurers a reason to keep offering plans. The Commonwealth Fund explains the danger of shrinking enrollment: “A smaller market would in turn discourage competition, since there would be less incentive for multiple insurers to offer coverage to fewer people” [10].
  • Because With fewer options, “the marketplaces would be more vulnerable to disruption if an insurer leaves.” [10]
  • So Sustaining coverage options reduces the risk of losing a workable plan and access to covered care. For an average American who relies on Marketplace coverage, that makes health protection more dependable.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: These personal benefits are conditional on Marketplace coverage. Census reports employment-based insurance covered 53.8 percent of the population for some or all of 2024. Credit eligibility excludes an affordable employer plan meeting minimum value and eligibility for the listed public programs; H.R.1834 does not change those conditions. The PROs state the buyer condition, and the job-loss and community-service routes have different reach. These facts inform applicability and strength; they do not contradict a benefit within the stated condition. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It helps sustain hospitals and clinics that serve the whole community.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It helps sustain hospitals and clinics that serve the whole community.

  • Because Coverage supports payment for care. An Urban Institute analysis of the enhanced credits links lower spending to “lower revenue for health care providers and fewer services rendered” [21].
  • Because A rural hospital analysis explains how falling revenue and more unpaid care threaten services for everyone: hospitals face “eliminating services that would affect all members of their community.” [22]
  • So More insured patients support paid care and reduce pressure to cut services. Preserving services protects [NAME]’s access to needed care, including while insured through work or Medicare.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The rural hospital estimate assumes 4.8 million more people uninsured in 2026. CBO, assuming January 2026 enactment, projects 0.1 million more insured in 2026 and 3.0 and 4.0 million in 2027 and 2028. Sources: [22], [3].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Restores larger Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax credits for monthly insurance payments for 2026–2028. CBO describes “an extension through 2028” [3], and the bill applies “to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [2] Compared with current law, CBO projects for 2028 “6.2 million more people would be enrolled through the health insurance marketplaces” [3] and “2.1 million fewer people would have employment-based coverage.” [3]

points.title: Restoring plans with no monthly payment renews an incentive for unauthorized enrollment that can interrupt care.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Restoring plans with no monthly payment renews an incentive for unauthorized enrollment that can interrupt care.

  • Because The enhanced credits provided “access to plans with no premium contributions for those earning 100 to 150 percent of the federal poverty level.” [23]
  • Because HHS linked the larger subsidies to misconduct: “the widespread availability of $0 premium plans created the incentive and opportunity for fraudulent and improper enrollments at scale” [24].
  • Because A missing bill helps hide unauthorized enrollment: “Because these enrollees do not receive a monthly premium bill requiring action on their part, they may not be aware they are enrolled.” [24] This keeps brokers paid: “This lack of awareness allows agents, brokers, and web-brokers to continue earning monthly commission payments from issuers for these enrollments.” [24]
  • Because Unauthorized enrollment and plan changes can cause “loss of access to medical providers and medications” [23].
  • Note The proposed $5 charge on automatic renewals was on hold before the vote. CMS’s September 2025 guidance lists it under provisions “Not In Effect for OE 2026 Due to Columbus v. Kennedy” [25] and says: “Qualifying consumers will continue to be automatically re-enrolled with no premium responsibility following application of Advance Payments of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC).” [25]
  • Because Unauthorized changes persisted under the safeguards already adopted. CMS reported: “In 2025, CMS estimates that approximately 200,000 consumers had their desired plan selection changed without their consent.” [26]
  • So Restoring this incentive increases exposure to unwanted coverage changes that can interrupt access to a doctor or medicine. For an average American enrolled in Marketplace coverage, avoiding such interruptions protects health and gives a reason to oppose the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish an increase in fraud-related interruptions of care under the law in force.

  • Because Plans with no monthly bill remain available to nearly all adults in the low-income group it cites: “Of adults who qualified for a free silver plan with enhanced premium tax credits, almost all (98%) would still qualify for a free bronze plan without enhanced premium tax credits.” [27]
  • Because The HHS account includes a monthly enrollment route: “individuals could be enrolled into these plans once every month through a special enrollment period (SEP) by predatory agents and brokers without the individual's knowledge.” [24]
  • Because Despite the hold on the $5 charge, CMS listed “Removal of Monthly Special Enrollment Period” [25] under provisions “In Effect For Open Enrollment (OE) 2026” [25].
  • Because The 2025 law also bars tax credits for enrollment based only on income outside the yearly signup period. CRS says it “disallows the PTC for individuals who enroll in an exchange plan during an SEP on the basis of expected household income” [28], starting with “plan years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [28]
  • Because From 2028, existing law “requires people to actively affirm their eligibility to enroll in marketplace coverage and to claim the premium tax credit when they apply for that insurance.” [29]
  • So The missing premium bill already exists for nearly all the cited group, while the bill does not restore the monthly enrollment route. The $5-charge hold and the 2025 case count do not establish that larger credits add interruptions of care under these rules.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CMS reports that for consumers with an unwanted plan change in 2025, it worked with issuers to confirm and restore their chosen plans. Sources: [26].

points.title: The projected shift away from employer coverage puts access to a needed doctor at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The projected shift away from employer coverage puts access to a needed doctor at risk.

  • Because Marketplace plans can leave a doctor outside every available plan. In its study of 2021 networks, KFF found: “On average, 27% of actively practicing physicians who submitted Medicare claims were not included in any Marketplace plan network offered to enrollees that year.” [18]
  • Because This creates a problem for people changing coverage: “This means that people transitioning to a Marketplace plan from another coverage source may not have been able to find any plan that included their doctor.” [18]
  • Because KFF’s 2023 survey found “adults with Marketplace coverage were more likely than those with employer-sponsored health insurance to report that a particular doctor or hospital they needed was not covered by their insurance (20% vs. 13%)” [18].
  • Because Those gaps affected care and health: “Among Marketplace enrollees who experienced this problem, 34% said that needed care was delayed, 34% said they were unable to get needed care, and 25% experienced a decline in health status.” [18]
  • So Replacing employer coverage with Marketplace coverage risks losing an established doctor and missing needed care. [NAME]’s wish to protect their health gives a reason to oppose that risk.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: KFF's network count measures whether providers are in a network, not whether they are available for appointments. Applying the benchmark credit to a gold plan can make more generous coverage relatively inexpensive. Sources: [18], [30].

Evidence note: A person claiming the credit must lack affordable job coverage, as CBO notes in a 2025 letter discussing people who lose credit eligibility. In a 2022 analysis of a permanent extension, CBO said the job-coverage decline is driven primarily by reduced employer offers and that few employers changed their decision under the temporary 2021–2022 subsidies. KFF says a narrow network may still provide adequate access. The deductible study followed one large self-insured firm moving from free care to a high deductible, and its estimated response is about a third of the RAND experiment's. Sources: [29], [31], [18], [32].

points.title: Replacing employer coverage with plans that pay less of treatment costs can put needed care out of reach.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Replacing employer coverage with plans that pay less of treatment costs can put needed care out of reach.

  • Because Standard Marketplace bronze and silver plans leave patients paying a larger share of treatment costs than typical employer plans: “Plans typically cover between 60 percent and 70 percent of an enrollee’s health care expenses — less generous than most ESI plans, which usually cover 80 percent or more.” [30] ESI means insurance through an employer.
  • Because The ACA’s extra help with deductibles and copayments ends above 250 percent of the federal poverty level: “However, CSR benefits disappear once income rises above 250 percent of FPL.” [30] CSR means this extra help with treatment costs.
  • Because Among plans studied in five regions, the cheapest bronze and silver plans “typically impose substantial financial barriers through high deductibles” [30]. A deductible is the amount a patient pays before insurance starts paying for services subject to it.
  • Because Higher deductibles can cause patients to cut useful care. A study followed a firm “which required all of its employees to switch from an insurance plan that provided free health care to a non-linear, high deductible plan.” [32] It found: “Consumers reduce quantities across the spectrum of health care services, including potentially valuable care (e.g. preventive services) and potentially wasteful care (e.g. imaging services).” [32]
  • So For workers moving into these plans without extra help with treatment costs, the bill’s coverage shift risks making illness harder to treat or prevent. [NAME] has a health reason to oppose that risk.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: KFF's network count measures whether providers are in a network, not whether they are available for appointments. Applying the benchmark credit to a gold plan can make more generous coverage relatively inexpensive. Sources: [18], [30].

Evidence note: A person claiming the credit must lack affordable job coverage, as CBO notes in a 2025 letter discussing people who lose credit eligibility. In a 2022 analysis of a permanent extension, CBO said the job-coverage decline is driven primarily by reduced employer offers and that few employers changed their decision under the temporary 2021–2022 subsidies. KFF says a narrow network may still provide adequate access. The deductible study followed one large self-insured firm moving from free care to a high deductible, and its estimated response is about a third of the RAND experiment's. Sources: [29], [31], [18], [32].

points.title: The coverage shift also risks leaving people without protection against dental disease.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The coverage shift also risks leaving people without protection against dental disease.

  • Because Employer benefits commonly include access to dental insurance. KFF reports: “According to the 2023 KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey, 90% of small firms and 94% of large firms offer dental insurance programs to their employees.” [33]
  • Because As of the vote, adult dental care was outside the ACA’s required medical benefits: “adult dental care is currently prohibited by agency regulation from being considered an EHB in individual and small group plans.” [33] EHB means a benefit those plans must cover.
  • Because Replacing lost employer dental benefits generally requires a separate payment that the restored credits do not cover: “adult enrollees must typically cover the full cost of premiums without subsidies.” [34]
  • Because Cost blocks dental care. KFF reports: “37% of Marketplace Enrollees Reported Delaying or Forgoing Dental Care Due To Cost Barriers” [33]. It explains: “Delaying needed dental care could lead to more serious health problems down the road.” [33]
  • So For people leaving employer dental benefits, subsidized Marketplace medical coverage leaves a separate bill to maintain dental protection. The bill’s shift away from employer coverage therefore creates a risk of gaps in dental care. Avoiding those gaps serves [NAME]’s wish to avoid disease.
points.con_html:
Response A fall in employer medical coverage does not establish the loss of employer dental benefits needed for this path to dental disease.

  • Because Most private dental benefits are separate from medical insurance: “only about 1.2% of commercial dental benefits are integrated into medical policies.” [35]
  • Because Federal rules allow dental benefits without employer medical coverage: “limited-scope vision or dental benefits can be provided without connection to a primary plan” [36].
  • Because Those separate benefits can coexist with Marketplace tax credits: “eligibility for excepted benefits does not preclude an individual from eligibility for a premium tax credit under section 36B of the Code” [36]. Here, excepted benefits include separate dental coverage.
  • Because The 37% figure is not a measure of dental benefits lost through a change in medical insurance: “Consumers having insurance coverage does not mean that all consumers surveyed had dental coverage.” [33]
  • So The PRO never connects the medical coverage shift to lost dental eligibility or employer dental payments. Without that link, it has not shown a new dental bill or an added risk of dental disease caused by the extension.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Restore the larger tax credits for buying Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace insurance for 2026–2028, compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026. The bill extends the rules “through 2028” and applies them to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [1] Assuming passage in January 2026, CBO estimates additional people insured: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.” [2]

points.title: More affordable coverage strengthens the country’s defense against contagious disease.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 More affordable coverage strengthens the country’s defense against contagious disease.

  • Because Coverage helps people get care. A study of previously uninsured adults eligible for Marketplace subsidies found “decreased barriers to medical care, increased the use of outpatient services and prescription drugs”. [3]
  • Because Cost barriers impede outbreak control. A COVID-19 modeling paper states that “financial barriers to COVID-19 care delayed diagnosis and exacerbated transmission.” [4]
  • Because Finding cases helps protect others: “COVID-19 testing allows case identification, initiation of isolation, contact tracing, and prompt treatment.” [5]
  • So By making coverage affordable for more people, the bill reduces a barrier to diagnosis and care. That strengthens outbreak control and protects people beyond those receiving the credits, advancing [NAME]’s concern for national protection against threats.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The COVID testing study measures insurance at the time of interview and warns that observational studies cannot prove causality. The pandemic paper models universal coverage eliminating patient costs. The addiction-benefit paper did not assess effects on treatment use. The Baltimore study notes that income changes can affect both insurance eligibility and treatment use. The emergency-department study covers the broader 2014 ACA expansions, including Medicaid. Sources: [5], [4], [6], [7], [8].

points.title: Supporting hospital finances helps preserve the country’s ability to respond to disasters and attacks.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Supporting hospital finances helps preserve the country’s ability to respond to disasters and attacks.

  • Because A comparison of keeping and losing the larger credits links their loss to “lower revenue for health care providers and fewer services rendered” and an “increase in uncompensated care sought by the uninsured”. Uncompensated care means care for which providers are not paid. [9]
  • Because Revenue losses at rural hospitals “could force hospitals to reduce costs by eliminating services that would affect all members of their community.” [10]
  • Because Small rural hospitals “are called upon to respond to a wide range of emergency situations in their communities”. Their emergency plans cover natural disasters and “Terrorism and bioterrorism events – bombings, use of biological agents such as anthrax”. [11]
  • So Supporting payments for care helps preserve hospitals and services that emergency responders need. That protects the country’s response capacity during disasters and attacks, including care for residents with other insurance.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The rural hospital estimate assumes 4.8 million more people uninsured in 2026. CBO, assuming January 2026 enactment, projects 0.1 million more insured in 2026 and 3.0 and 4.0 million in 2027 and 2028. Sources do not identify which emergency services would change. Sources: [10], [2].

points.title: Broader coverage strengthens the country’s response to the opioid crisis.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Broader coverage strengthens the country’s response to the opioid crisis.

  • Because Marketplace plans must “offer substance use disorders benefits at parity with medical and surgical benefits”, meaning comparable insurance protections for addiction treatment. [6]
  • Because Insurance helps people reach treatment. A study identifies “Financial barriers such as lack of insurance coverage” as an obstacle. In its long-term study of Baltimore residents who injected drugs, private insurance “was associated with receipt of buprenorphine and having a regular source of medical care.” Buprenorphine is a medicine for opioid addiction. [7]
  • Because Medicines for opioid addiction, including buprenorphine, have “proven effectiveness at reducing mortality risks.” [12]
  • Because An earlier ACA study, covering states with and without Medicaid expansion, found: “Areas with higher uninsurance rates prior to the ACA saw larger reductions in opioid-related ED visits after the ACA took effect.” These are emergency department visits; the study found the effect emerged over several years. [8]
  • Because The national health-security strategy identifies substance use disorder as a challenge to communities’ ability to withstand crises and states: “Community resilience plays a significant role in national health security.” [13]
  • So Making treatment coverage more affordable strengthens the response to a deadly drug threat and supports communities’ ability to withstand further emergencies. Both serve [NAME]’s concern for a secure country.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The COVID testing study measures insurance at the time of interview and warns that observational studies cannot prove causality. The pandemic paper models universal coverage eliminating patient costs. The addiction-benefit paper did not assess effects on treatment use. The Baltimore study notes that income changes can affect both insurance eligibility and treatment use. The emergency-department study covers the broader 2014 ACA expansions, including Medicaid. Sources: [5], [4], [6], [7], [8].

points.title: Better access to care helps preserve the workforce the country depends on.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Better access to care helps preserve the workforce the country depends on.

  • Because Research on the larger credits describes improved access to care, including “primary and preventive care visits”, which “can both help prevent and manage costly chronic diseases.” Chronic diseases are long-lasting illnesses. [14]
  • Because These illnesses affect the wider economy. CDC researchers identify “lost productivity in the workforce” among their burdens. [15]
  • So Supporting care that prevents and manages illness helps preserve people’s ability to work. That supports the country’s ability to produce goods and provide services, strengthening its stability.

points.title: Maintaining health-care spending supports jobs, economic stability, and public services.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Maintaining health-care spending supports jobs, economic stability, and public services.

  • Because Coverage losses cut provider income: “Health care providers that lose revenue must reduce how much they can spend on their staff and goods purchased from vendors”. [16]
  • Because The effects spread beyond health care: “Reductions in labor expenses mean that some jobs are lost and some staff may be paid less. Thus, staff must restrict their purchases of consumer goods”. [16]
  • So Restoring the credits supports payments to providers, workers, and suppliers, reducing a source of economic disruption across the country.
  • Because Falling incomes also weaken public finances: “The combined reductions in individual and business incomes inevitably lead to lower state and local tax revenues.” [16]
  • Because The resulting budget pressure hinders public services: “This means that state and local governments will have more difficulties balancing their budgets and paying for health, human service, and other government functions.” [16]
  • So Supporting employment and incomes also protects the revenue governments use to serve residents. This chain supports both national stability and the state’s capacity to protect its people.
points.con_html:
Response The spending study does not establish that the bill preserves jobs and tax revenue across the country, rather than supporting a particular flow of spending.

  • Because It uses the “IMPLAN economic modeling system” [16]. USDA’s guidance warns: “Results of the analysis, whether output or jobs, should not be reported as net, new, or additional.” [17] Jobs supported by spending are not a count of jobs the country would otherwise lose.
  • So The model’s provider, supplier, and worker spending chains do not establish the claimed national employment and tax gains from this bill. The further claim about protecting public services rests on those unestablished gains. This does not deny that the affected providers and workers would receive the payments.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The jobs study's spending assumptions were aligned with the cost of extending the credits and reversing other changes in 2026, so its comparison does not isolate H.R.1834. Sources: [16].

points.title: Lower premium bills support household spending and economic stability.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Lower premium bills support household spending and economic stability.

  • Because An analysis of the credits’ expiration links higher insurance bills for people who stay covered to less spending elsewhere: “This reduces their ability to purchase other goods and services, further dampening state economies.” [16]
  • So By lowering premiums for eligible policyholders, the bill preserves money for other purchases. That supports households and the businesses that depend on their spending, strengthening economic stability across the country.
points.con_html:
Response More purchasing power for policyholders does not by itself establish a more stable national economy.

  • Because The model’s own guidance says: “Input-Output models do not account for general equilibrium effects such as offsetting gains or losses in other Industries or geographies or the diversion of funds from other projects.” [18] These are changes elsewhere when money and work shift between uses.
  • So Policyholders do keep more money for other purchases. Following that purchasing power alone leaves out the changes needed to establish the claimed national effect.

points.title: Federal premium help reduces pressure to divert limited state funds to replace it.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Federal premium help reduces pressure to divert limited state funds to replace it.

  • Because Connecticut committed its own money to replace lost federal help before the January vote: “Connecticut allocated an additional $51 million after a November 2025 special legislative session”. [19]
  • Because Filling that gap competes with other health protection. California and Colorado shifted state subsidies away from reducing deductibles and copayments to reducing premiums: “switching from a program that lowered out-of-pocket cost sharing (by reducing or eliminating deductibles and copayments) to one that lowers monthly premiums to help people purchase and maintain comprehensive coverage.” [19]
  • So Restoring federal help meets more of that premium need and reduces pressure on states to fund replacements. That protects states’ ability to use limited health funds for other needs, serving [NAME]’s concern for a capable state.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The April 2026 report says seven states modified their subsidy programs in response and that the new state investments were for 2026 only. It also reports Massachusetts adding $250 million. Connecticut's allocation came after a November 2025 session. Sources: [19].

points.title: A more affordable insurance system outside work helps the country withstand economic downturns.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 A more affordable insurance system outside work helps the country withstand economic downturns.

  • Because Job losses can remove health protection: “Because insurance coverage in the U.S. is closely tied to employment, economic downturns pose a serious threat to Americans’ access to affordable health care.” [20]
  • Because People losing job-based coverage can use the Marketplace outside its yearly enrollment window. CMS explains: “You’ll have 60 days to enroll in a Marketplace plan from the time your coverage ends, which may or may not be the last day of employment.” [21]
  • Because CBO projects lower prices before tax credits for the plans used to set subsidy amounts in 2027–2029 because “on average, the people who enroll in the marketplaces would be healthier than would be the case” without the extension. [2]
  • Because This wider sharing of medical costs benefits people without subsidies too: “Even those not eligible for PTCs see lower premiums with enhanced PTCs because the additional enrollment has improved the nongroup market risk pool.” PTCs are premium tax credits; a risk pool is the group whose medical costs insurance shares. [22]
  • So The bill makes an available route to coverage outside work more affordable, through larger credits and lower insurance prices. That helps the country absorb job losses without also losing as much health protection, strengthening its ability to withstand economic shocks.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO substitutes lower prices and higher enrollment for evidence of fewer coverage gaps when people lose jobs.

  • Because CBO’s forecast of lower prices in 2027–2029 rests on the expectation that “on average, the people who enroll in the marketplaces would be healthier than would be the case” [2] without the extension. That is a forecast about the mix of enrollees, not coverage transitions during a downturn.
  • Because Research on the earlier ACA using 2014–2019 data found that “the risk of losing insurance remained virtually unchanged with the introduction of the landmark ACA.” [23] It draws the distinction explicitly: “These results underscore how policies that increase the share of people with insurance at a point in time do not necessarily increase the stability and certainty associated with having insurance.” [23] It studies the earlier ACA, not the enhanced credits.
  • So A price and enrollment forecast cannot substitute for evidence about keeping or quickly replacing coverage after job loss. The closest evidence cited here does not show that subsidized Marketplace access reduced that risk.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill restores larger federal tax credits for Affordable Care Act health insurance for 2026–2028: “H.R. 1834 would authorize an extension through 2028 of the premium tax credit structure” [2]. It applies from 2026: “The amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [1]. CBO's January-enactment estimate puts the added deficit for 2026–2035 at $80.582 billion; its table, in millions of dollars, reports “80,582” [2]. Those added deficits mean more federal borrowing.

points.title: The added debt puts more pressure on funding for defense and emergencies.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The added debt puts more pressure on funding for defense and emergencies.

  • Because More debt raises the government's exposure to interest costs: “the larger debt is, the more an increase in interest rates raises debt-service costs.” [24]
  • Because CBO connects debt to limits on national protection: “Lawmakers might feel constrained from using federal tax and spending policies to respond to unforeseen events or for other purposes, such as to promote economic activity or strengthen national defense.” [24]
  • Because CBO also warns of harm to the U.S. role abroad if lawmakers become “reluctant to increase spending to prepare for or respond to an international crisis” [24].
  • So The bill adds debt and interest demands that put defense and crisis response under greater budget pressure. Preserving the state's ability to prepare for threats and defend citizens gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added pressure.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

points.title: The added borrowing increases exposure to a financial crisis that would threaten national stability.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The added borrowing increases exposure to a financial crisis that would threaten national stability.

  • Because An August 2025 budget update from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget included the July budget law and new tariffs. It projected debt growing faster than national output: “Debt held by the public will rise from about 100 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ($30 trillion) today to 120 percent of GDP ($53 trillion) by 2035.” [25]
  • Because CBO explains the risk of that path: “The likelihood of a fiscal crisis would increase if federal debt continued to grow faster than GDP, because mounting debt could erode investors’ confidence in the U.S. government’s fiscal position.” [24]
  • Because A loss of confidence would raise interest rates and lower the value of existing government bonds. CBO says losses to banks and other investors “could be large enough to cause some financial institutions to fail.” [24]
  • Because The damage could spread as banks lend less: “such a crisis could spread globally as liquidity declined and financial institutions reduced their lending, leading to an economic contraction.” [24]
  • So The bill adds to the debt burden behind this crisis risk. Protecting the country against financial breakdown and economic disruption gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added exposure.

points.title: The added debt threatens financial tools the United States uses to protect its interests.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The added debt threatens financial tools the United States uses to protect its interests.

  • Because Growing debt creates risks beyond a sudden crisis. CBO identifies “a gradual decline in the value of Treasury securities and other domestic assets, heightened expectations of inflation, and a loss of confidence in the U.S. dollar as the dominant international reserve currency.” [24] This includes the dollar's role as the main currency other countries hold in reserve.
  • Because CBO explains the funding consequence: “Such developments would make it more difficult to finance public and private activity.” [24]
  • Because The national security strategy calls U.S. financial markets “pillars of American influence that afford policymakers significant leverage and tools to advance America’s national security priorities.” [27]
  • So Adding debt adds risks to stable funding and financial influence that support U.S. security. [NAME]'s concern for a strong, secure country gives a reason to oppose those risks.

points.title: The added borrowing competes with investment that supports military strength.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The added borrowing competes with investment that supports military strength.

  • Because CBO explains the mechanism: “The increased federal borrowing associated with larger amounts of debt reduces the resources available for private investment.” [24]
  • Because Less investment weakens production over time: “That reduction in private investment would slow economic growth.” [24]
  • Because The national security strategy calls the economy “the necessary foundation of our military.” [27]
  • So The bill's borrowing puts pressure on investment and production that sustain national defense. Protecting that economic foundation gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.

points.title: Interest paid abroad reduces the national income available to sustain U.S. strength.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Interest paid abroad reduces the national income available to sustain U.S. strength.

  • Because CBO identifies a separate cost of growing debt: “Rising interest costs associated with federal debt would drive up interest payments to foreign holders of that debt and thus decrease national income.” [24]
  • Because The national security strategy identifies the economy as a source of resources for security: it “generates wealth we can invest in strategic interests” [27].
  • So Added borrowing carries an income cost through interest paid abroad, beyond its effect on domestic investment. Retaining national resources that support the country's strength gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that cost.

points.title: The larger subsidies put more public money within reach of organized fraud.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 The larger subsidies put more public money within reach of organized fraud.

  • Because The enhanced credits expand fully paid coverage for eligible low-income households: “The reduction in applicable percentages allows households with incomes between 100% and 150% of FPL to receive full subsidies, reducing consumers' premium contributions to zero dollars.” [28] FPL means the federal poverty level.
  • Because CMS links this feature to abuse: “the widespread availability of $0 premium plans created the incentive and opportunity for fraudulent and improper enrollments at scale” [29].
  • Because Income-check gaps remained in the rules for 2026. CMS explained that a planned check was paused: “Income DMIs will not be opened for applicants when the Marketplace attempts to verify an applicant’s attested projected annual household income with the IRS, but the IRS returns no tax data.” [30] That means missing tax records would not trigger this extra income check.
  • Because A November 2025 conviction shows an actual loss from organized enrollment fraud. The Justice Department reported a scheme seeking “over $233 million in fraudulent ACA plan subsidies for which the federal government paid at least $180 million.” [31]
  • So Restoring larger subsidies expands the money and incentives exposed to a proven fraud mechanism. A strong state must keep public resources from financing crime. [NAME] therefore has a reason to oppose this added exposure.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO carries an older fraud warning into 2026 without separating larger credits from a monthly signup route that had ended.

  • Because The agency running the federal insurance Marketplace (CMS) links abuse to repeated signups: “By fully subsidizing the premium for these plans, individuals could be enrolled into these plans once every month through a special enrollment period (SEP) by predatory agents and brokers without the individual's knowledge.” [29]
  • Because Before the vote, CMS listed “Removal of Monthly Special Enrollment Period (SEP)” [30] among the rules already in force. This was the signup route for people with income at or below 150 percent of the federal poverty level.
  • Because The 2025 law also bars tax credits for special signups based on income alone from 2026. Congress's research service describes the bar on “an SEP on the basis of expected household income” [32] that is “not connected to a change in circumstances specified by the HHS Secretary.” [32] It “applies to plan years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [32]
  • Because H.R.1834 extends the credit rules. Its credit changes concern “Extension of Rules To Increase Premium Assistance Amounts” [1] and “Extension of Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [1].
  • So Extending the credit amounts does not reopen that route. A past theft and larger lawful payments do not establish extra money reaching criminals under those rules. This response does not answer the PRO’s point that an income check was paused for 2026.

CMS estimates that about 200,000 consumers had a desired plan changed without consent in 2025, after the July 2024 control. CMS says it worked with issuers to restore those selections. Sources: [33], [34].

points.title: Expanding fully paid plans makes unauthorized enrollment harder to notice and exposes citizens to disrupted care.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Expanding fully paid plans makes unauthorized enrollment harder to notice and exposes citizens to disrupted care.

  • Because CMS explains how fully paid plans conceal unauthorized signups: “Because these enrollees do not receive a monthly premium bill requiring action on their part, they may not be aware they are enrolled.” [29]
  • Because A planned $5 charge on automatic renewal had been paused before the January vote. CMS stated: “Qualifying consumers will continue to be automatically re-enrolled with no premium responsibility following application of Advance Payments of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC).” [30]
  • Because GAO documented the scale of reported unauthorized signups and switches: CMS received “approximately 275,000 complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35]
  • Because GAO explains that these practices can cause “loss of access to medical providers and medications” [35]. The November 2025 conviction also established harm: “some of these consumers experienced serious disruptions in their medical care and often lost their prior insurance coverage under Medicaid or other programs.” [31]
  • So By expanding plans that hide unauthorized enrollment, the bill increases exposure to organized abuse that can interrupt care. Protecting citizens from that threat through a reliable national insurance system gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html:
Response The complaint history does not establish added hidden enrollment or disrupted care from this extension under the consent controls already in place.

  • Because CMS changed controls for existing coverage on the federal Marketplace: “Beginning July 19, 2024, CMS began blocking agents and brokers from making changes to a consumer’s FFM enrollment unless the agent or broker is already associated with the consumer’s enrollment.” [36]
  • Because CMS provides a way for a new broker to act with the consumer's involvement: “the consumer must conduct a three-way call with the Marketplace Call Center” [36].
  • Because Congress's audit agency, GAO, combines “complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35] That period includes months before these controls began.
  • So The control acts before an unassociated broker can switch existing coverage; it does not depend on a premium bill exposing the switch afterward. The complaint total mixes initial enrollments and switches across different safeguards. It does not establish added harmful switches from this extension under the rules in force on January 8. This response concerns switches of existing coverage; it does not address new unauthorized enrollments.
