pages.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
pages.description: H.R.1834 would have extended for three years the enhanced health insurance subsidies that help people buy private coverage through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. The extension would have kept these subsidies available to households earning more than four times the federal poverty level, who would otherwise have lost them.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, H.R.1834 restores larger tax credits—help paying for ACA health insurance—for 2026–2028. CBO says it “would authorize an extension through 2028” [1]. The bill makes the changes apply to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [2] It also extends the “Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [2], restoring access to help above four times the poverty line. Assuming January enactment, CBO projects more people insured than under current law: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028” [1].

points.title: It puts the inherited Christian duty to care for sick and poor neighbors into practice.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It puts the inherited Christian duty to care for sick and poor neighbors into practice.

  • Because The Southern Baptist confession teaches: “We should work to provide for the orphaned, the needy, the abused, the aged, the helpless, and the sick.” [3]
  • Because The National Association of Evangelicals applies that duty to public funding: “Adequate funding for food, shelter and health care should be maintained so that those who cannot care for their families and themselves receive the support they need.” [4]
  • Because The larger credits bring coverage within reach of low-income households: “With the enhanced subsidies, most enrollees at the lowest income level — under 150 percent of poverty — pay little or nothing for their plan.” [5]
  • Because Coverage helps people receive care: “health insurance is essential to getting timely health care in the United States” [5].
  • So Restoring this help carries an established Christian duty into public policy, giving [NAME] a reason grounded in following religious tradition.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The premium tax credit itself continues without the bill; only the enhancements lapse. The U.S. Catholic bishops' October 2025 letter urges Congress to extend the enhanced credits while barring their use for plans covering elective abortion. H.R.1834 extends them without that bar. Sources: [6], [7], [2].
points.retirement_reason: Access to care for poor and sick people is the substantive benefit. Religious endorsement does not create a distinct Tradition reason.

points.title: It helps families practice the Christian duty to protect life before and after birth.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps families practice the Christian duty to protect life before and after birth.

  • Because The coverage made more affordable includes care during pregnancy and after birth: “Maternity care and newborn care — services provided before and after a child is born — are essential health benefits.” [8]
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession teaches: “We should speak on behalf of the unborn and contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death.” [3]
  • So Making this coverage easier to keep helps families obtain care for mothers and babies, putting their inherited belief in the protection of life into practice.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: All qualified health plans must cover maternity and newborn care under either option, and Medicaid pays for nearly half of U.S. births. Sources: [8].
points.retirement_reason: Maternal and prenatal health are the substantive benefits; this argument does not connect them to continuing a particular religious observance or family custom.

points.title: It lowers a cost of keeping a mother at home for children’s religious upbringing.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It lowers a cost of keeping a mother at home for children’s religious upbringing.

  • Because Insurance costs compete with household needs. An enrollee warned that losing the larger credits would mean “digging into basic necessities, like, food, car, gas, rent.” [9]
  • Because Caring for children at home is a practice the religious right values: “Focus on the Family has always taken pains to express and provide support for mothers who choose to stay home with their young children.” [10]
  • Because Focus on the Family connects that role to passing on faith: “God created us to have relationship with Him. The most effective place for us to learn that is not at church — it’s at home!” [11]
  • So For eligible families using ACA insurance on one wage, the bill lowers the cost of keeping a mother at home to care for children and teach the faith.

points.title: It reduces a loss of insurance help that marriage can trigger at the income cutoff.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It reduces a loss of insurance help that marriage can trigger at the income cutoff.

  • Because The income cutoff can penalize two people who qualify separately but cross the married cutoff when their incomes combine. Heritage explains that “the FPL for a couple is less than twice that for a single person” [12]. FPL means the poverty line used to set the cutoff.
  • Because The bill extends the “Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [2].
  • So For otherwise eligible couples whose insurance costs qualify for help above that limit, marrying no longer causes all aid to disappear merely because their combined income crosses it.
  • Because The comparison must also count what the couple would receive unmarried. Consider two childless adults, each with $46,950 in annual income counted for the credit: 300% of the “$15,650” [13] one-person amount. Married, their $93,900 is 443% of the “$21,150” [13] two-person amount, above the cutoff. Hold their plans fixed, with benchmark premiums totaling $20,000 a year. Under ordinary 2026 credits, the table reads “At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” [14], so they pay about $9,352 unmarried and the full $20,000 married: a $10,648 cost of marrying. Under the restored schedule, “300 | 0.0600” [15] means about $5,634 unmarried, and “400 or more | 0.0850” [15] means about $7,982 married: a $2,348 cost. For this couple the bill lowers the cost of marrying by about $8,300.
  • Because Evangelical teaching opposes “creating economic disincentives to marriage.” [4]
  • So Reducing this financial obstacle for such couples supports the traditional practice of marriage.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that premium credits can produce both marriage penalties and bonuses. Under the bill, the cost of marrying falls for some couples crossing the income cutoff (support point 4's example: about $8,300 lower) and rises for some couples below it (oppose point 9's example: about $1,729 higher). Both examples rest on stated assumptions. Sources: [16], [14], [15].

points.title: It helps families fulfill the biblical duty to honor aging parents.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It helps families fulfill the biblical duty to honor aging parents.

  • Because Removing the income cutoff particularly helps older people who rely on ACA insurance: “The cliff—and therefore this disparate treatment—falls disproportionately on older people, those in high-premium areas (which are heavily rural areas), and small business owners.” [17]
  • Because Focus on the Family explains the duty this way: “Honor implies choosing to give great respect and care to our elders” [18].
  • Because That care includes material help: “This might mean sharing your home and offering financial support.” [18]
  • So Lower insurance bills for these parents reduce the cost they and their families must meet, helping families carry out the inherited duty to honor and care for them.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Focus on the Family names financial support as one possible way to honor a parent and also says, 'There is no verse in Scripture that obligates you to take aging parents into your home or cancel your vacation plans to pay for their prescriptions.' The cliff source identifies older buyers as an age group and does not report how often their children help with these costs. Sources: [18], [17].
points.retirement_reason: Helping relatives care for elderly people is a general care justification here; no particular inherited arrangement or observance supplies an additional premise.

points.title: It supports church giving and paid ministry, helping congregations continue worship and teaching.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It supports church giving and paid ministry, helping congregations continue worship and teaching.

  • Because Small churches use ACA coverage for staff: “Among the most affected are small congregations that usually can’t afford group plans and instead provide salary stipends to staff members for use in the ACA Marketplace” [19].
  • Because A Christian clergy relief fund tied its proposed emergency aid to the larger credits: “If Congress renews the subsidies at the 2025 levels, the program will not move forward.” [20]
  • So Restoring those credits eases the strain on pastoral families and churches that help pay their insurance costs.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession makes regular giving a religious duty: “According to the Scriptures, Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.” [3]
  • Because Higher insurance bills also squeeze giving. A pastor reported: “Riverside Church is projecting 20% attendance growth but flat giving for 2026 as more dollars go to health insurance instead of tithing” [19].
  • So Lower bills leave members more room to continue customary giving and support their congregation.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession says Sunday observance should include “exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.” [3]
  • So Easing these pressures on church budgets helps sustain the clergy, worship, and teaching through which congregations practice and pass on their faith.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The clergy relief fund's program is a one-time $2,500 stipend for up to 1,000 clergy. The Riverside Church figure is one congregation's forecast of 20% attendance growth with flat giving for 2026. Sources: [20], [19].

points.title: It helps Christian health ministries continue their healing work.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It helps Christian health ministries continue their healing work.

  • Because The Catholic Health Association links lost coverage to unpaid care: “the loss of coverage would put additional stress on local health care providers as they face more uncompensated care and bad debt.” [21] These are bills providers do not collect.
  • Because Church clinics also face added demand for free care. Reporting from Bread of Healing at Cross Lutheran Church explains: “They are bracing for higher demand as more residents are expected to forgo insurance as a crucial tax credit is set to expire and premiums spike.” [22]
  • Because Catholic providers identify care for those in need as their religious mission: “Our health ministry is especially committed to serving those most in need, recognizing that our mission is not complete until quality, affordable, and accessible health care is a reality for all.” [21]
  • So Keeping more patients insured eases unpaid bills and the added demand for free care, helping Christian institutions carry on an established ministry.

points.title: It reduces financial pressure to give up inherited family farms and rural ways of life.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It reduces financial pressure to give up inherited family farms and rural ways of life.

  • Because Minnesota Farmers Union warned that higher insurance costs were “forcing some to choose between buying health insurance, making their operating loan payments or in some cases, putting food on the table” [23].
  • Because In a 2003 statement on agriculture, U.S. Catholic bishops identify the threatened inheritance: “They are about a way of life for farm families in the United States who are unable to meet debt payments and face selling a farm that has been in the family for generations.” [24]
  • Because The bishops defend preserving this life: “We stand with farmers, particularly those who own small and family farms here and abroad, in their struggle to live with dignity, to preserve a way of life, and to strengthen rural communities.” [24]
  • So Lower insurance costs leave farm families more money to meet farm debts, helping them keep the land and work through which they pass on family and rural customs.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The bishops' statement on family farms dates from November 2003 and concerns farm debt, not insurance. The Minnesota Farmers Union statement is from October 2025 and refers to independent family farmers generally. Sources: [24], [23].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.1834?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, the bill restores larger tax credits for buying Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace insurance in 2026–2028. It replaces “through 2025” [2] with “through 2028” [2] and applies to “taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [2] CBO projects “6.2 million more people would be enrolled through the health insurance marketplaces” [1] in 2028.

points.title: It makes plans covering a practice rejected by the religious rule against abortion easier to buy.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It makes plans covering a practice rejected by the religious rule against abortion easier to buy.

  • Because Some states have “laws that require all fully-insured group plans and individual plans (including Marketplace plans) to include abortion coverage.” [25]
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession directs believers to “speak on behalf of the unborn and contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death” [26].
  • So Larger credits lower the price of entering plans with abortion benefits. For [NAME], continuing the particular religious rule against abortion supplies a reason to oppose making coverage of that practice easier to obtain. This justification concerns that religious observance, rather than a general appeal to protect vulnerable life.
  • Note Federal credits cannot pay the abortion portion of the premium beyond the rape, incest, and life-endangerment exceptions: “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” [25] The objection concerns cheaper entry into plans that include those benefits.

points.title: It increases public payments to plans that religious teaching tells taxpayers not to support.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It increases public payments to plans that religious teaching tells taxpayers not to support.

  • Because The Catholic bishops object to paying for the plan itself: “federal taxpayer dollars are still paying for the plans that cover abortion” [27]. Their October 2025 letter asks Congress to pair extension with a limit: “We urge Congress to extend the enhanced PTCs while amending all PTCs to disallow their being used for plans that cover elective abortion.” [7] H.R.1834 contains no such limit.
  • Because The Southern Baptist public-policy commission says “no taxpayer’s conscience should be violated by being forced—even indirectly—to pay for abortions.” [26]
  • So Larger credits increase public support for the plans these religious bodies reject. Preserving their rule against indirect support gives [NAME] a reason to oppose those added payments, regardless of whether abortion numbers rise.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The premium tax credit itself continues without the bill; only the enhancements lapse. The U.S. Catholic bishops' October 2025 letter urges Congress to extend the enhanced credits while barring their use for plans covering elective abortion. H.R.1834 extends them without that bar. Sources: [6], [7], [2].

points.title: It increases the financial pressure to accept a personal payment for abortion coverage.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It increases the financial pressure to accept a personal payment for abortion coverage.

  • Because Plans covering abortions beyond those exceptions must collect an abortion-coverage payment of “at least $1 per enrollee per month” [28] and “deposit these separate payments into segregated accounts” [28].
  • Because Where state law requires Marketplace plans to cover abortion, buying one includes that payment. KFF describes the mandate as covering “individual plans (including Marketplace plans)” [25].
  • Because Christian health-sharing ministries state the religious concern as getting care “without being forced to fund procedures or drugs that violate their conscience.” [29]
  • So Where every Marketplace option includes this charge, refusing it means giving up Marketplace aid. The bill increases the aid a believer must forgo. Preserving the practice of refusing payments that violate religious teaching gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that pressure.
points.con_html:
Response A state coverage mandate alone does not establish that an objecting buyer has no subsidized plan without elective abortion coverage.

  • Because Washington law says, “No individual or organization with a religious or moral tenet opposed to a specific service may be required to purchase coverage for that service or services if they object to doing so for reason of conscience or religion.” [30]
  • Because A 2023 survey of Marketplace plans identifies an actual exception: “Oregon, one of the states requiring that abortion be covered, has granted an exemption to plans sponsored by religious health systems.” [31]
  • So The PRO must establish its no-acceptable-plan condition for the relevant buyer and coverage year. A count of states with mandates does not establish that condition. These examples do not show that every buyer has an acceptable option.

points.title: It broadens access to plans with gender-transition benefits that traditional Christian teaching opposes.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It broadens access to plans with gender-transition benefits that traditional Christian teaching opposes.

  • Because Washington’s required benefits still include this care: its benchmark plan “requires individual and small group health plans to cover gender-affirming treatment.” [32]
  • Because Southern Baptists teach that “gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [33] and declare that “we oppose efforts to alter one’s bodily identity” [33].
  • So Cheaper enrollment opens access to these plans’ transition benefits. Maintaining this religious understanding of sex gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
  • Note The 2026 federal rule shifts the excluded benefit’s cost to the state: “the state is required to defray the cost of the benefit.” [32] Washington appropriated money “so that the benefit can continue to be offered.” [32] Larger federal credits still make the plan carrying that state-funded benefit easier to buy.

points.title: It widens access to IVF practices that endanger embryos protected by the tradition.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It widens access to IVF practices that endanger embryos protected by the tradition.

  • Because Illinois includes in vitro fertilization (IVF), fertilizing eggs outside the body, in its required individual-plan benefits: “IVF and other fertility treatments are covered on individual and small-group plans” [34].
  • Because IVF can leave embryos frozen in storage. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine describes a route to their destruction: “Facilities may dispose of unclaimed embryos by removing them from storage and thawing without transfer.” [35]
  • Because Southern Baptists teach that human beings deserve protection “from the moment of fertilization until natural death” [36] and object to the “continued freezing, stockpiling, and ultimate destruction of human embryos” [36].
  • So Larger credits make coverage of IVF easier to obtain, widening access to practices that expose embryos to this danger. Following the inherited duty to protect embryonic life gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].
points.retirement_reason: The stated objection is protection of embryonic life, rather than the distinct marital-conception rule in the next point. Religious endorsement of protection alone is insufficient.

points.title: It widens access to IVF that Catholic tradition rejects for replacing the spouses’ sexual union.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It widens access to IVF that Catholic tradition rejects for replacing the spouses’ sexual union.

  • Because The Illinois Marketplace benefits described above include IVF: “IVF and other fertility treatments are covered on individual and small-group plans” [34].
  • Because The Catholic bishops describe IVF as “joining egg and sperm in a glass dish, not in the mother’s body” [39].
  • Because Their teaching draws the moral line at replacing the marital act: “procedures that assist the marital act in being procreative are morally acceptable, while those that substitute for it are not.” [39]
  • So Cheaper access to IVF expands access to a substitute for marital intercourse. Preserving this Catholic teaching on how spouses should conceive children gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose the bill, apart from embryo destruction.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].

points.title: It expands access to contraception rejected by traditional Catholic teaching on marriage.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It expands access to contraception rejected by traditional Catholic teaching on marriage.

  • Because Most private plans must “cover, without any cost sharing, the full range of FDA-approved contraceptives and services” [40]. Covered birth control therefore comes without a separate patient charge under the rule.
  • Because The Catholic bishops teach that “every act of intercourse must remain open to life and that contraception is objectively immoral.” [41]
  • So Larger credits expand access to plans with these benefits. Within Catholic traditionalism, maintaining this teaching about married sex gives [NAME] a reason to oppose widening access to contraception for preventing pregnancy.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].

points.title: It gives Marketplace insurance a larger price advantage over Christian mutual aid.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It gives Marketplace insurance a larger price advantage over Christian mutual aid.

  • Because The credits pay for “health insurance obtained through the marketplaces established by the Affordable Care Act.” [1] Health care sharing ministries (HCSMs) fall outside that insurance system: “HCSMs are not health insurance” [42].
  • Because For eligible buyers, subsidies can make Marketplace coverage “significantly less expensive than an HCSM membership” [42].
  • Because These ministries practice religious mutual aid: “Members affirm shared faith commitments and contribute to each other’s medical bills, supported by prayer and mutual encouragement.” [29] Christian Healthcare Ministries links this practice to “the command of Galatians 6:2” [43].
  • So For households receiving larger credits, the bill cuts Marketplace payments while ministry dues receive no credit. This gives them a stronger financial reason to choose insurance instead of contributing through a ministry. Preserving the religious practice of sharing medical bills, giving, and prayer gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added incentive.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].

points.title: It increases the financial cost of marriage for some couples buying Marketplace insurance.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 It increases the financial cost of marriage for some couples buying Marketplace insurance.

  • Because Marriage combines the couple’s incomes for the credit. The law requires that “the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year.” [44]
  • Because For 2026 coverage in the 48 contiguous states, the poverty-line amounts used for credits are “$15,650” [13] for one person and “$21,150” [13] for two. Two married adults therefore face a lower poverty-line amount than two separate one-person tax households.
  • Because The ordinary 2026 premium-share table reads: “At least 250% but less than 300% 8.44% 9.96% At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” [14]. Thus the share is 8.44% at 250% of poverty and 9.96% at 369%.
  • Because The bill restores the enhanced schedule. Its IRS table gives “250 | 0.0400” [15] and “369 | 0.0773” [15]: shares of 4% and 7.73%. To find the income percentage, IRS instructions say to “drop any numbers after the decimal point.” [15]
  • So Consider two childless adults, each with $39,125 in annual income counted for the credit. Compare being unmarried throughout 2026 with being married throughout 2026. They are otherwise eligible all year. Hold their plans and full premiums fixed, with premiums high enough to receive credits. Separately, each is at 250% of poverty; married, their $78,250 is counted at 369%. Under ordinary 2026 credits, their combined annual premium share rises from about $6,604 to $7,794 when married—a $1,190 cost. Under the restored schedule, it rises from $3,130 to about $6,049—a $2,919 cost. The bill adds about $1,729 to this couple’s annual cost of being married rather than unmarried.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession calls marriage “the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime” [45] and “the framework for intimate companionship, the channel of sexual expression according to biblical standards” [45].
  • So Maintaining this marriage tradition gives [NAME] a reason to oppose increasing the money such couples lose by marrying.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that premium credits can produce both marriage penalties and bonuses. Under the bill, the cost of marrying falls for some couples crossing the income cutoff (support point 4's example: about $8,300 lower) and rises for some couples below it (oppose point 9's example: about $1,729 higher).
